title: USWNT roster vs. Spain: Takeaways as Sanchez return highlights Hayes' squad
description: U.S. women's national team head coach Emma Hayes has named a 26-player roster for two friendlies against world champion Spain.
fullText:
U.S. women's national team head coach Emma Hayes has named a 26-player roster for two friendlies against world champion Spain.

The 2027 World Cup is growing ever closer, with Spain set to defend its title and the USWNT looking for redemption after a shocking round-of-16 exit in 2023.

Hayes has named a roster featuring a mix of mainstays and newcomers, with some NWSL standouts getting their first call-ups after excellent club seasons.

The USWNT will face Spain on Oct. 10 at Audi Field in Washington D.C., and will then head north for a rematch at Subaru Park in Chester, Pennsylvania on Oct. 13.

Here are three takeaways from the USWNT's October roster.

It's been nearly two years since Ashley Sanchez played for the USWNT, but her form with the North Carolina Courage was too good to ignore.

Sanchez has scored 20 goals this season, tying the NWSL's all-time record for a single campaign. It's been an eye-opening breakout for a player whose previous career high in goals was five.

The 27-year-old's resurgence comes at a perfect time as the World Cup closes in. Sanchez will be hoping for a chance to banish her demons from 2023, when she was called into the World Cup roster but didn't play a single minute in Australia and New Zealand.

The USWNT has a ridiculous amount of depth on the front line, but Sanchez has a big chance to prove herself in training and in the Spain matches.

Hayes has been focused on expanding her player pool since the 2024 Olympics but as the World Cup nears, she is still handing opportunities to new players rather than closing ranks.

The latest example comes in the form of three first-time call-ups on this roster: Evelyn Shores, Trinity Byars and Pietra Tordin.

Shores has been a two-way standout at left back for Angel City, but is listed as a midfielder on this roster. It will be interesting to see where Hayes sees the 21-year-old fitting in.

Tordin and Byars, two forwards with extensive U.S. youth international experience, have both taken the leap this season with the Portland Thorns and San Diego Wave, respectively.

Byars has scored 10 goals while providing excellent No. 9 play, while Tordin profiles as more of a playmaking forward. The 22-year-old has tallied seven goals and nine assists, linking up well with her now-international teammate Sophia Wilson.

It would be hard to fathom a USWNT roster without Naomi Girma or Mallory Swanson, but that had seemed at least somewhat possible in recent weeks.

Both players have endured difficult stretches at the club level, but they have still been called into this roster. It's not surprising to see them with the USWNT, but they'll both have more to prove than usual.

Swanson has just two goals in 11 appearances for the Chicago Stars this season, and recently returned from a month out with injury. The Stars are far and away the worst team in the NWSL, so it's hard to know how much Swanson's struggles are a product of her surroundings.

It's safe to say Girma's move to Chelsea has been a disappointment so far, as the central defender has struggled through various injuries. This season, the 26-year-old has yet to play a single minute for the Blues. Though she has dealt with a calf injury, right now Girma is available and simply isn't being selected.

title: Muharemović scores as Bosnia and Herzegovina claim first Nations League win
description: Tarik Muharemović scored his second international goal as Bosnia and Herzegovina secured an impressive 4-2 victory over Romania in the UEFA Nations League.The Leeds United defender started at centre-...
fullText:
Tarik Muharemović scored his second international goal as Bosnia and Herzegovina secured an impressive 4-2 victory over Romania in the UEFA Nations League.

The Leeds United defender started at centre-back and played the full 90 minutes at Bucharest's Arena Naţională, helping his side claim their first win of the Nations League campaign.

Armin Gigović had put Bosnia and Herzegovina ahead before Muharemović doubled their advantage in the 19th minute, heading home from a corner for his second international goal.

Daniel Bîrligea pulled one back for Romania before Haris Tabaković restored Bosnia and Herzegovina's two-goal lead before half-time.

Muharemović played a key role in the victory, making 60 touches and completing 36 accurate passes.

The 23-year-old also produced an impressive defensive display, recording a match-high 17 defensive contributions. He made two tackles, two blocks, nine clearances and four interceptions, while also making five recoveries and winning five duels.

The result leaves Bosnia and Herzegovina with four points from their opening two Nations League fixtures, following Friday's goalless draw with Poland.

Next up for Muharemović? Bosnia and Herzegovina host Gabriel Gudmundsson's Sweden on Friday night in Zenica.

title: Strain making most of Bairns lifeline
description: Football has a funny way of making things fall into place - and Ryan Strain's signing feels like a case in point.  The Australia international's arrival raised a few eyebrows among the Bairns faithful earlier this summer.  It soon became clear Adams was injured and needed surgery, which explained the decision to bring in Strain.
fullText:
Football has a funny way of making things fall into place - and Ryan Strain's signing feels like a case in point.

The Australia international's arrival raised a few eyebrows among the Bairns faithful earlier this summer. That was no slight on Strain's ability.

We had already brought in Jack McMillan at right-back while Keelan Adams, a key performer in recent years, was also on the books.

It soon became clear Adams was injured and needed surgery, which explained the decision to bring in Strain. He had spent the first part of the summer at PFA Scotland's inaugural free agent training camp, but has since wasted little time making an impression at Falkirk.

Of the 17 players we brought in over the summer, Strain has arguably been the standout so far.

Others have impressed too, but the 29-year-old has slotted seamlessly into the right-back role and made it his own.

His influence seems to grow by the week. He's set up a goal in two of his past three outings, offers a threat with his set-piece delivery and has been reliable at the back, while his 14 tackles won is the joint highest in the Premiership.

Ironically, now that everyone is available again, it feels like his jersey to lose.

title: Wales without seven players for World Cup play-off
description: Ceri Holland is one of seven players who will miss out through injury when a depleted Wales squad take on Albania in their Women's World Cup play-off semi-final next month.
fullText:
Ceri Holland is one of seven players who will miss out through injury when a depleted Wales squad take on Albania in their Women's World Cup play-off semi-final next month.

Influential midfielder Holland has not been included in the Wales squad having been sidelined for Liverpool's past three games.

Wales will also be without Olivia Clark, Hayley Ladd, Laura Hughes, Ffion Morgan, Ella Powell and Mia Ross due to fitness issues.

Head coach Rhian Wilkinson has handed first senior call-ups to two 18-year-olds, Newcastle United forward Casi Gregson and Tottenham Hotspur wide player Heidi Hills.

Wales travel to Albania for their play-off semi-final first leg on Friday, 9 October before the return in Llanelli four days later.

The winners will face either Norway or Romania in the play-off final in December.

Should Wales come through both play-off rounds, they may then have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs early next year to seal a place at next year's World Cup in Brazil.

Women's World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

The lowest-ranked of the eight play-off winners in Europe will go into the inter-confederation play-offs, and - should they get that far - there is a decent chance that would be Wales.

The loss of Holland for the Albania ties is a significant blow given her importance to Wilkinson's team, with the 28-year-old becoming arguably Wales' most important player since the retirement of Jess Fishlock in 2025.

The absence of Leicester City's Clark means Safia Middleton-Patel, who is on loan at Watford from Manchester United, is the only goalkeeper with any international experience in this Wales squad.

Crystal Palace player Ladd – who has 115 caps - Southampton midfielder Hughes and West Ham wide player Morgan could all have expected game-time in the Albania matches.

Ross, who is unattached after leaving Charlton Athletic earlier this month, and Bristol City's Powell both got minutes in Wales' most recent camp, when they drew in Montenegro and then beat the Czech Republic in June to seal top spot in their World Cup qualifying group.

Wales are unbeaten in their past eight internationals having endured a run of 12 games without a win which ended with a friendly success against Switzerland in December 2025.

Gregson and Hills are among six uncapped players in the squad, alongside goalkeepers Soffia Kelly and Poppy Soper, Wolves' Olivia Francis and 19-year-old centre-back Cadi Rodgers, who joined Plymouth Argyle this week having most recently been at Chelsea.

Gregson, from Ceredigion, is a former Gwalia United player who moved to Newcastle in February.

Tottenham academy product Hills, who was previously at Reading, is promoted to the senior Wales squad having received her first under-19s call-up earlier this year.

title: Fifa accuses Uefa of 'misinformation campaign'
description: Uefa's suggestions that Fifa president Gianni Infantino "violated any law or ethical principle are categorically without merit" says world football's governing body.
fullText:
World football's governing body has accused its European counterpart of a "misinformation campaign", while refusing to hand over files relating to shelved plans to sell stakes in the World Cup.

Uefa last month filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

Uefa accused Fifa president Gianni Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" and "a fraudulently off-market price promoted by [him] for his own benefit" over the now-shelved Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme.

In its response on Monday, Fifa said Uefa's filing contained "numerous false or misleading statements about Fifa and Infantino".

"With no basis whatsoever, Uefa suggests that Mr Infantino sought to profit personally from the FFE proposal," Fifa said in a filing in the Southern District of Florida, opposing Uefa's motion for discovery.

"Uefa's suggestions that Mr Infantino violated any law or ethical principle are categorically without merit."

It also described Uefa's filing as "farcically overbroad", saying "districts faced with similar requests have outright rejected such applications".

Fifa also described Uefa's conduct as "in bad faith and for the purpose of harassment".

Making clear it was refusing to release evidence relating to the FFE plan, Fifa said it "respectfully requests that the court deny Uefa's application for discovery."

BBC Sport has contacted Uefa for comment. BBC Sport has been told insiders believe if Fifa has nothing to hide, it should disclose the documents and speed up the legal process.

Uefa has led the rebellion against the Fifa president, who is facing calls to stand down from three confederations.

Fifa's FFE plan proposed selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, sparking a major backlash.

Infantino faced calls for his resignation but claimed the project had been intended to generate additional money for the game.

Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan, and called for an independent review of FFE.

Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

title: Red Roses to return to Sunderland for Women's Six Nations
description: England will return to Sunderland's Stadium of Light – the venue for their record-breaking Women's Rugby World Cup opener – for the 2027 Six Nations.
fullText:
England will return to Sunderland's Stadium of Light - the venue for their record-breaking Women's Rugby World Cup opener - in their first home match of the 2027 Six Nations.

The Red Roses will play Scotland at the venue on 17 April.

It will be the first time they have played a home match away from a rugby-specific ground outside of a World Cup.

England drew 42,723 fans to the Stadium of Light for the 67-9 victory over the United States that opened the Women's Rugby World Cup in August 2025.

That attendance surpassed the 42,579 who watched the final of the previous edition as the Women's Rugby World Cup's biggest crowd.

The Red Roses subsequently smashed that mark again with an 81,885 sell-out for their final victory over Canada at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

England's 2027 Six Nations campaign also includes home matches against Italy at Northampton's DPD Stadium at Franklin's Gardens on 24 April and a final-round meeting against France at Twickenham on 15 May.

The venues for their away fixtures against Wales and Ireland are yet to be announced

"It was an amazing atmosphere to be a part of - one of the favourites in my career," England full-back Ellie Kildunne said of her previous visit to the Stadium of Light.

"I just remember the noise when we got off the bus and the amount of time the fans stayed behind afterwards. It was incredible. They really spurred us on that night.

"If the match with Scotland can replicate anything close to that night, it's sure to be another memorable occasion."

England are aiming for their ninth successive Six Nations crown.

Their preparations for the tournament will begin after they play two Tests against Canada and one Test against the United States on the away leg of their WXV Global Series campaign next month.

title: Inside Liverpool's increasing global investment in youth
description: Liverpool are becoming increasingly proactive in their search for global young talent. BBC Sport takes a closer look.
fullText:
Liverpool may have made three signings worth more than £100m each over the past two summers in Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola, but internally there is a realisation that after a significant amount of young talent was sold last summer, the club need to replenish that talent pool.

Since 2020, Liverpool have made more than £230m from selling players who have represented them at youth level and that has been a major part of owner Fenway Sports Group's self-sustaining business model, with the funds reinvested into the club.

Since Brexit, there is a 'premium' on young English players and it is why Liverpool's global talent department, led by Matt Newberry since the winter of 2024, now have a major role to play.

Fifa rules state that international transfers of players are only permitted if the player is over 18 and, since Brexit, Premier League clubs are no longer permitted to sign players under 18 from European countries.

Newberry's team is responsible for deciding which young talents from overseas should be targeted for a move. Using their wealth of contacts across the world, including dedicated regional scouts, Liverpool are becoming increasingly aggressive in the space.

It helps that new sporting director Julian Ward is well known for his global network.

"Any player we sign, the first intention is that we want them to play in the first team and there's a belief that there's a chance for everyone that signs here," Alex Inglethorpe, Liverpool Academy director told BBC Sport.

"That really is no different since the impact of Brexit on the English market, which is quite significant. There's now a premium on young English players. Time will tell if that premium is worthwhile but it's definitely a change.

"So it's fairly natural for a club like Liverpool to look within Merseyside in the first instance then broaden that out - national recruitment happens at 14 and after that you look globally, which is what we've done."

Mor Talla Ndiaye's journey began in the Senegalese village of Sandiara where he played football in the streets.

He progressed through the ranks playing for Bousports Academy in the town of Thiadiaye before joining Amitie Football Club in the city of Thies.

Come January this year, Liverpool fended off interest from other European clubs and signed the 18-year-old for about £1m plus add-ons.

"You have access to certain talent based on points accrued from playing homegrown players. We had a couple of ESC (elite significant contribution) spots to explore the wider market and that's something which, even prior to Brexit, was a fairly normal thing," Inglethorpe adds.

Ndiaye is a left-footed centre-half who played for Liverpool in pre-season under Andoni Iraola and was an unused substitute in three games in the second half of last season under Arne Slot.

"He's an incredible story, isn't he? From where he's come from to where he is - and he's such a humble kid. He's an unbelievable lad to work with," Rob Page, Liverpool's U21 boss, told BBC Sport.

"There's exciting times ahead but he's got a lot of work to do. He's nowhere near the finished article but he's on the right path. His attitude is spot on and he's at the club that will definitely help him develop."

At Liverpool, there is an optimism regarding Ndiaye and a genuine belief that if he makes it to the top, it could be one of the great football stories.

Liverpool opened discussions with his academy and his agency, Sport Cover, after scouts spotted his performances at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last winter and several video calls were arranged before the club's representatives travelled to Senegal.

Once there, they visited where Ndiaye trained, as well as meeting the people that supported his development before presenting their vision to him directly.

A round-table meeting was organised with his family to help understand his environment, the story and the context in which he grew up.

Ultimately, Ndiaye chose Liverpool because they offered the clearest pathway and their approach in getting to know him stood out.

Ndiaye isn't the only player to have been identified and recruited by Liverpool's global talent team.

After the U17 World Cup, Liverpool also made a £2.6m move for another centre-half, Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

Ndukwe was impressive in pre-season and the 18-year-old Austrian has gone on loan to Levante in La Liga as he looks to obtain a UK work permit.

The list doesn't stop there. Samuel Martinez, the 17-year-old Colombian midfielder, will join next summer after having "30 offers from around the world, external", according to his father.

It doesn't always work. Arsenal beat Liverpool to the signing of Andria Bartishvili from Georgia last month and the 17-year-old will join the Gunners next summer when he is 18.

But the moves for Martinez and Ndiaye showcase Liverpool's willingness to spread beyond Europe and into areas they may not have explored before. Given the inevitability of other top clubs circling emerging talent, the idea of selling the pathway that Liverpool offers is imperative.

Since arriving, Ndiaye has settled in with a host family - which is normal when players aren't from the area - that are used to working with Liverpool.

"Players come from varying parts of the world and, when someone comes in and doesn't speak much English at the start, you have to help with that and help understand culturally the differences in food, the weather and even the pitches you play on," Inglethorpe said.

"There's a lot of understanding in terms of the level of support that's needed and the most important thing you can give a young player is the time.

"I'm delighted that Mor made such a strong impression and he's done as well as he has, but we hope that he's going to get better and better as he continues to adapt."

This summer, Liverpool also confirmed moves for Lucca Brughmans, the 18-year-old Belgian goalkeeper, and Djylian N'Guessan, the 18-year-old French forward, with both set to join the club permanently in 2027.

In the modern game, most talents are known and there aren't many hidden gems anymore, but Liverpool believe that by digging deeper and wider they can get ahead of the curve, using their global network and their reputation as a club that will help players develop.

title: Top 14 award winner Willis reiterates desire to play Test rugby
description: Jack Willis, who last played for England at the 2023 Rugby World Cup,  retains his award as the best player in France.
fullText:
Jack Willis, who last played for England at the 2023 Rugby World Cup, jokingly challenged reporters to find him a way back into Test rugby after he retained his award as the best player in France.

Willis moved to Toulouse in November 2022 after Wasps went out of business, and was initially given dispensation to continue playing for England given the exceptional circumstances.

The back row won the most recent of his 14 caps in a pool-stage hammering of Chile, but, having opted to remain in French club rugby, has not been eligible for England since.

A long-standing policy restricts England selection to domestic-based players. It strengthens Prem clubs' ability to retain top talent, while England also benefit from increased access and control over their players.

Willis has been a huge success across the Channel. He was named player of the match in June's Top14 final win over Montpellier as he added a fourth French title to the Champions Cup crown he lifted in 2024.

Willis came top of a three-man shortlist for the Top14's best player for the 2025-26 campaign, seeing off competition from France and Bordeaux-Begles fly-half Matthieu Jalibert and Clermont-Auvergne's All Black Harry Plummer.

Willis becomes only the second player - after France captain Antoine Dupont - to retain the accolade.

The 29-year-old made his decision to stay at Toulouse, where his contract runs until 2029, despite knowing it would put him out of contention for an England spot.

"You know what you sacrifice," Willis said of his Test career.

"It's something I still want to do, but rules are rules."

Willis is now, in theory, available for selection by Ireland.

Three years have passed since he last appeared for England and, under World Rugby's 'birthright' rule, he could now represent a country which he, his parents or his grandparents were born in. Willis' grandfather was born in Belfast.

Ireland's strong preference for home-based players has been relaxed on rare occasions in the past with Jonny Sexton and Tommy Bowe continuing to play for their country despite moves to Racing 92 and the Ospreys respectively.

However, the likes of Simon Zebo have also found themselves excluded after heading overseas.

It is highly unlikely any compromise would be found that allows Willis to play for Ireland while remaining with Toulouse.

"I'm a quarter Irish, but they have the same rules as England," said Willis.

"You need to do some digging, that's your job, you find the way [around the rules]!"

title: Ex-England captain Dallaglio to sell World Cup winner's medal
description: Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio is set to sell his 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal after being declared bankrupt.
fullText:
Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio is set to sell his 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal after being declared bankrupt.

The 54-year-old has put a number of items from his illustrious career up for auction including medals, trophies and caps.

The World Cup medal is expected to raise between £50,000 and £80,000 while in total the collection has an estimated value of £180,000.

Dallaglio was one of the stars of the England side that won the World Cup in dramatic fashion against Australia 23 years ago.

Other items up for sale include a British and Irish Lions cap, his 1993 World Cup Sevens winner's medal and a 2003 Six Nations Championship winner's medal.

During an appearance on The High Performance podcast, external earlier this month, Dallaglio spoke about his bankrupcy.

He said: "As a result of getting divorced, I was made bankrupt.

"I had some financial problems - I could've done things a lot better."

He also said he sought therapy after his divorce and bankruptcy left him wallowing in "self-pity".

The auction at Budd's, external in Northamptonshire takes place on 13 October.

title: Life bright for Gilmour after baseball and World Cup heartache
description: Scotland midfielder Billy Gilmour opens up on the pain of missing out of this summer's World Cup.
fullText:
Billy Gilmour sits at Lesser Hampden, a beaming smile bursting across his face.

The topic of conversation is revolving around him missing the World Cup in the summer, something that could have been defined by harrowing disappointment and regret.

Instead, the Napoli midfielder's face lights up when asked about a night at the baseball in Miami, where the injured Scotland ace was asked to hobble on to the field and hurl the ceremonial first pitch.

"I was nervous," Gilmour tells BBC Scotland, recollecting the evening at the Miami Marlins against the Texas Rangers.

"I was just so happy it wasn't a crap throw, or it was bouncing. It was some experience."

How Manzambi became one of Europe's best young talents

Listen: Can Scotland shock the Swiss at Hampden?

Pocognoli has no concern over Scotland's lack of goals

The maturity and level-headedness of the 25-year-old defies his years.

Just days before he was due to jet off to the United States with the Scotland squad for the first men's World Cup the nation had experienced since before he was born, a crushing blow.

In the farewell game at Hampden against Curacao, he suffered a knee injury that would mean he was left behind. While a body blow to Steve Clarke, his squad and the country, it would have been devastating to a young man with the world stage at his feet.

He admits those initial days were difficult as reality set in, but Gilmour seized the chance to become a supporter across Boston and Miami with his family around him.

"The boys fell on top of me and I've heard something straight away," he said of the injury. "Typical, try to run it off, make sure it was okay.

"It was tough. You have to take yourself away for a couple of days and I did.

"I got to go away for a bit, just kind of switch off and it happened, so I had to deal with it. When you're there around the squad, you try to be as best as you can, as positive as you can.

"When you think of it, how lucky you still are to get to go there and watch the games and be with family and family holiday also."

Gilmour added: "I would be with the team some nights, but the squad and Robbo [captain Andy Robertson] and the gaffer, Steve Clarke, at the time, he basically said: 'Look, if it's too much to come in, don't come in. Stay as much time with the family. Go and experience it with the fans'."

Gilmour was still in Miami when news broke of Clarke's resignation as Scotland head coach. He's a man the Napoli midfielder acknowledges he owes so much to after giving him his debut in 2001.

Now, however, it's the Sebastien Pocognoli era and the former Rangers, Chelsea and Brighton & Hove Albion man seems central to it.

In the 0-0 draw in Slovenia on Saturday, it was Gilmour who caught the attention during a resurgent second half for the Scots.

He is often seen as more of a deep-lying central midfielder, but there was a different dynamic to his game with the absence of club-mate Scott McTominay, who is recovering from a heart procedure.

"When I was younger, I really liked playing higher up, trying to be among it," Gilmour, who is set to feature at Hampden on Tuesday against Switzerland - live on the BBC, said.

"Whenever I get asked to play on the pitch, as long as I'm on the pitch, I'm happy. I just want to play football and enjoy it."

Now 25, there is plenty time to make new memories in a Scotland shirt. Yet, with so many young faces coming into the squad, the Ayrshire man is probably now a senior figure in the group.

It's something he says he embraces, although Gilmour is coy about the prospect of maybe taking on the armband whenever current captain Robertson decides to pass it on.

"For me, it's everyone's dream to be a captain at a club or a country," he said.

"Of course I'd be really proud to, but Robbo's my captain and he's a really good captain as well.

"What he's done for Scotland is incredible and he's very close on the record [most caps held by Kenny Dalglish] and I'm sure he'll get it."

title: Toone and Kelly miss out on Lionesses squad

The Lionesses face Greece in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off matches in October.

"I had those conversations with them and that was very hard to take. They took it well and of course, they want to work on that."

On reports suggesting Kelly's absence may have been linked to an injury, Wiegman added in her media conference: "I had the conversation with Chloe and for me, it was just what I saw on the pitch. I kept that with football with her."

In addition, Chelsea forward Aggie Beever-Jones and Arsenal duo Lotte Wubben-Moy and Taylor Hinds have not made the 23-player squad.

Captain Leah Williamson returns having missed June's 4-0 defeat by Spain and 3-0 win over Ukraine.

"I think she's played really well in the last few weeks and at the start of the season. She is happy and you can see," added Wiegman.

title: How FIBA 3x3 Basketball Went From A Business Case To An Olympic Sport
description: FIBA 3x3 basketball evolved from a Youth Olympic experiment into a global sport, driven by gender equity, digital engagement and a spectator-first approach ahead of LA28.
fullText:
(This is part one of a two-part story based on a Forbes exclusive interview with Alex Sanchez on September 22, 2026. All quotes are taken directly from a transcript of the interview.)

In 2010, Alex Sanchez was not trying to save basketball, reinvent basketball or even necessarily build a new Olympic sport. He was doing something much more familiar to the world of business. He was analyzing an investment opportunity.

At the time, FIBA 3x3 basketball was being played at the Youth Olympic Games, but the International Basketball Federation wanted to know whether the abbreviated version of basketball was something more than a novelty. Could three-on-three basketball become a legitimate sport with its own athletes, competitions, commercial potential and global audience? Sanchez, who had an MBA from the University of Chicago and a background in private equity, venture capital and consulting, was asked to find out.

Sixteen years later, that analysis looks remarkably prescient.

Three-on-three basketball is now an Olympic sport, and it will arrive in Los Angeles for the 2028 Olympic Games with FIBA Managing Director Alex Sanchez still helping guide its global development.

"I did the analysis," Sanchez recalled in an interview with Forbes. "At the end of it … my conclusion at the time was that there was a real business case to develop 3x3 as a standalone discipline."

But there was an even bigger possibility. Sanchez concluded that 3x3 could become an Olympic sport if FIBA did the right things.

Sanchez's path to FIBA was not the conventional route for a basketball executive. Born in Barcelona to a Spanish father and German mother, Sanchez attended a German school in Spain and developed what he describes as two cultural perspectives on the same things. Before joining FIBA, he had already lived and worked in several European countries, including Spain, Belgium, Germany and the United Kingdom. He eventually came to the United States to earn an MBA at the University of Chicago, attracted in part by the finance-driven approach of the university's business program. After graduate school came private equity, venture capital and consulting.

The organization's previous secretary general wanted an objective analysis of 3x3. The sport was appearing at the Youth Olympic Games, but FIBA wanted to know whether there was a sustainable business proposition underneath it. Sanchez deliberately approached the assignment without treating it as a basketball project.

"I analyzed it as it would be a new brand for shoes or a new engine for planes," he said.

That distinction mattered. Instead of asking whether basketball fans liked three-on-three basketball, Sanchez was essentially asking whether a new sporting property could create a sufficiently differentiated product, audience and business model. The answer was yes. The next question was much harder: What would FIBA have to build to give 3x3 a legitimate opportunity to become Olympic? Sanchez and his colleagues produced a concept paper laying out what would have to happen.

That roadmap would require much more than changing the number of players on the court.

One of the first strategic decisions was gender equity. From the beginning, FIBA wanted men's and women's 3x3 to develop together. Sanchez said the organization was determined that national-team competitions would include men and women at the same time so the women's side would have an opportunity to grow at a comparable pace. The strategy was straightforward: If women's 3x3 were treated as an afterthought, it could fall behind.

Instead, gender equity became part of the architecture of the sport.

The second major milestone was professional competition. FIBA needed to demonstrate that 3x3 was not simply something athletes played occasionally at a Youth Olympic event. It needed professional athletes competing year-round. That led to the launch of the FIBA 3x3 World Tour in 2012, less than two years after FIBA's board decided to pursue the discipline. For Sanchez, this was critical.

"It had to have its own professional competition league tour," he explained.

The World Tour provided something that a collection of exhibition events could not: evidence that 3x3 could support a professional sporting ecosystem. It showed that athletes could make 3x3 their sport rather than treating it as a side activity.

And it gave FIBA an increasingly visible international product.

The next challenge was perhaps the most fundamental: What exactly should 3x3 basketball be?

FIBA could simply have taken traditional basketball, removed two players from each side and played the game on a half court. Instead, Sanchez said FIBA deliberately adapted the rules. The goal was to bring the organized version of the game closer to the way people actually played street basketball. That philosophy eventually became central to the sport's identity.

"The idea was to put the spectator in the center of all our changes or all our decisions," Sanchez said.

The objective was not simply to preserve basketball's traditional form. It was to create an experience. FIBA eventually described 3x3 with a simple phrase: "most thrilling urban sport." That phrase captured the strategy. The venues mattered. The rules mattered. The pace mattered. The presentation mattered.

And even the equipment became part of the product.

FIBA developed a ball specifically for 3x3. It is smaller than a traditional men's basketball but heavier, a combination Sanchez said was designed around the characteristics of the game and particularly outdoor grip and shooting. That might sound like a small detail.

The creation of a dedicated 3x3 ball was another indication that FIBA was no longer treating the discipline as simply a modified version of five-on-five basketball. It was becoming its own sporting product.

Perhaps the most interesting part of Sanchez's 3x3 strategy is that the sport was being designed for spectators before smartphones became the dominant way many younger fans consume sports. Today, that approach looks almost obvious.

A 3x3 game takes place on a half court with six players on the floor. The action is compact. The games are short. And the format naturally produces frequent highlights. Sanchez believes those characteristics make 3x3 particularly well suited for mobile viewing.

"You actually can see them everywhere," he said, referring to the short games and abundance of highlights.

That became an important part of FIBA's digital strategy. The organization created a social-media operation specifically focused on producing clips, polls and other digital content for platforms including Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and TikTok. The target audience was especially important. Sanchez said the core social audience falls largely within the 13-to-35 age range.

The sport therefore wasn't simply being played for the audience sitting courtside. It was also being packaged to be consumed by the person watching on a phone.

According to Sanchez, FIBA 3x3 now has more than 10 million social-media followers. Its dedicated social-media channels generate well above 1 billion views annually, according to Sanchez, approaching 2 billion views. Those figures are part of the story of how an experimental discipline became a global sporting property. But Sanchez believes another characteristic is just as important.

The audience is geographically distributed.

Rather than being concentrated primarily in one continent, Sanchez said 3x3 has developed meaningful participation and interest across Europe, the Americas and Asia. That distribution is rooted in something deceptively simple. A basketball hoop and a basketball are enough to begin.

As Sanchez put it, "if you have a ball and you have a hoop, actually, basically everybody will end up" trying to play.

That accessibility may be one of 3x3's greatest advantages.

For many basketball players, three-on-three is not something they learned from a federation. It is something they discovered after school at a park, in a driveway, or on an outdoor court with friends. The rules may vary. The competition may be informal. The stakes may be nothing more than bragging rights. But the fundamental experience is remarkably universal.

The beauty of the game was its simplicity. You didn't need a full roster, a coach or an elaborate facility. You needed a ball, a basket and somebody willing to play.

FIBA has taken that intuitive experience and built a professional sport around it without destroying the essence of the game.

title: Protect College Sports Act passes U.S. Senate vote, House next up
description: The Protect College Sports Act aims to create some concise solutions to the wild world of college football and other collegiate sports. The U.S. legislative measure is now one step closer to becoming a reality. On Monday night, the U.
fullText:
The Protect College Sports Act aims to create some concise solutions to the wild world of college football and other collegiate sports. The U.S. legislative measure is now one step closer to becoming a reality.

On Monday night, the U.S. Senate pushed forward the PCSA with a 77-22 vote. However, voting in the House of Representatives still needs to take place in order to clear both chambers of Congress.

The PCSA has become a talking point in college sports over recent months with NIL and transfer portal chaos creating significant issues in football, college basketball and other sports. President Donald Trump has been making his rounds at sporting events, including Texas' win over Tennessee at Neyland Stadium this past weekend.

Trump's been a major proponent for the bill, and Texas senator Ted Cruz recently suggested that the U.S. president will sign the bill live on ESPN's College GameDay if it passes the Senate and House.

MORE: Senators propose coach salary cap for Protect College Sports Act

United States President Donald Trump is shown on the video board at Neyland Stadium before the game. Mandatory Credit: Randy Sartin-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Top conferences like the Big Ten and SEC have heavily pushed for the act to move forward with NIL's uncertainty. Many programs are having issues navigating the new world of college sports with players leaving schools yearly.

Cruz and Washington senator Maria Cantwell co-wrote the bipartisan bill, which is a step closer to hitting the House floor. Meanwhile, CBS Sports indicates that could be months away with the House of Representatives reportedly not scheduled to return until November 9.

"This bill puts an end to the chaos plaguing college athletics," Cruz said Monday. "It protects NIL opportunities because student-athletes deserve the opportunity to benefit from their talent without being taken advantage of by unscrupulous agents and backdoor deals … It prevents the most powerful and wealthy conferences from breaking away to form a super league. But most importantly, it protects our student-athletes."

The biggest aspects of the bill that are being pushed include transfer and eligibility rules, as well as NIL regulations. Meanwhile, NCAA antitrust protection is another sticking point as the governing body looks to restore order with athlete compensation.

MORE: Ted Cruz plans for Donald Trump to sign Protect College Sports Act on ESPN show

The clock is still ticking on the PCSA, though, considering a new Congress is sworn in January 3. It's not impossible for Congress to get a deal done prior to that date, but time is certainly running quickly.

title: Astros weren't great in regular season, but neither were these teams that reached World Series
description: The Astros are the first team with a .500 record to make the MLB postseason. They can look this list of teams who also underachieved in the regular season, but got hot at the right time.
fullText:
You know what they call a team with a mediocre regular season record that gets hot at the right time and wins the World Series? Champions.

That's all the Houston Astros care about as they enter the postseason with the distinction of being the sport's playoff-qualifier with the fewest wins in a complete 162-game schedule.

Still, they're in the postseason, which means, beginning with Tuesday's start of the wild-card series against the Chicago White Sox, they're 14 victories away from winning a World Series that brings with it a banner that will fly just as high and a trophy that will shine just as bright as the other two in franchise history.

If the Astros need any encouragement, they can look at history and find plenty of teams who had discouraging regular seasons, but found their stride in October and went all the way to the World Series.

Here are the teams with the worst regular seasons that still made it to the end…

Lost World Series
Before the current version of the Astros came along, the Mets and the 2005 San Diego Padres owned the record for playoff teams with the fewest wins in a full regular season. Unlike the Padres, the Mets, led by 1973 Cy Young Award winner Tom Seaver and managed by Yogi Berra, made it all the way to the World Series. The Mets, who became known for Tug McGraw's catchphrase "Ya Gotta Believe!!!", were in last place with a month to play and five games below .500 on Sept. 11 before winning 12 of their final 16 games. They beat the vaunted Big Red Machine of the Cincinnati Reds in the NLCS and had a 3-2 series lead on the Oakland Athletics before dropping Games 6 and 7 to lose the World Series.

Won World Series
The Cardinals, whose .516 winning percentage is the lowest for any World Series champion, had two separate eight-game losing streaks - by comparison, the Astros lost eight in a row once in April - and a seven-game losing streak, but still outpaced the Astros by 1 ½ games in a weak National League Central. They went on to shock the San Diego Padres in the NLDS and take out the New York Mets in a seven-game NLCS before coasting past Justin Verlander and the Detroit Tigers in just five games in the World Series. The light-hitting David Eckstein was named World Series MVP for hitting .364 against the Tigers.

Lost World Series
The Diamondbacks narrowly earned a wild-card spot despite getting swept by the Astros in the regular season's final series, which the Astros needed to edge out the Texas Rangers in the AL West. Arizona upset the Brewers in the wild-card series, then swept the Dodgers in the NLDS despite finishing 16 games behind them in the NL West. The Diamondbacks, who were led offensively by current Astros first baseman Christian Walker, needed seven games to beat the Phillies in the NLCS before finally succumbing to the Rangers, who had eliminated the Astros in a tense seven-game ALCS.

Won World Series
Before the 2006 St. Louis Cardinals came along, this Twins team was the worst to win a World Series. The Kirby Puckett-led Twins went just 29-52 on the road in the regular season but used the raucous Metrodome to their advantage in the postseason, winning all four home games over the St. Louis Cardinals in the World Series. The Twins still are the only team with a losing run differential in the regular season to go on and win the World Series. The Twins were outscored by 20 runs in the regular season, while the current Astros were outscored by 32.

Won World Series
It's tough to think about any of those Yankees teams that three-peated from 1998-2000 as not great, but the last team of that title run limped to the finish, losing 15 of its final 18 games while still managing to hold off the Boston Red Sox for a playoff spot. Once the Yankees were in, though, they got hot and beat the Athletics in a thrilling five-game ALDS before finishing off the Mariners in six games in the ALCS. With Andy Pettitte and Roger Clemens leading the pitching staff, the Yankees crushed the Mets in a Subway World Series that included Clemens chunking a broken bat at Mets slugger Mike Piazza during Game 2.

Lost World Series
Cleveland was the beneficiary of playing in a weak American League Central where no other team finished above .500 that season. Still, Cleveland had a potent offense with Jim Thome, Matt Williams and David Justice each hitting more than 30 home runs. Cleveland went through the Yankees and Orioles in the playoffs before falling to the Florida Marlins in a thrilling seven-game World Series that ended with a walk-off single from Édgar Rentería.

Lost World Series
Astros fans all know what ultimately happened to this Phillies team, but it was a feat that it even made it this far. Philadelphia got off to such a poor start that manager Joe Girardi was fired in June. Under interim manager Rob Thomson, the Phillies went 65-46 the rest of the way to make the playoffs by one game. From there, they eliminated the Cardinals, Braves and Padres before running into the Astros, who had won 106 regular-season games and finished off Philadelphia in six games.

Won World Series
The 2014 World Series pitted two teams that didn't reach 90 wins in the regular season with the 89-73 Kansas City Royals falling to the 88-74 Giants. That Giants team didn't have much of an offense with no one one the team reaching 25 home runs or 90 RBIs, but it rode the arm of Madison Bumgarner in the postseason. Bumgarner, who threw a complete-game shutout in Game 5 of the World Series and came back to throw five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, pitched a remarkable seven times in that playoff run, putting up a 1.03 ERA in 52 ⅔ innings.

Won World Series
Astros fans are plenty familiar with this team. The Braves entered the postseason with the worst record of anyone in the playoffs that year. They were 5 games out in August, but went 36-18 over the final two months of the regular season and kept that hot streak going in the postseason, including beating the 95-win Astros in six games in the World Series. Jorge Soler, who hit a ball completely out of the Astros' home ballpark, was named World Series MVP.

There's more to Houston with the Chronicle.

title: Australia-born Strange in England World Cup squad
description: Australia-born second-row forward Jasmin Strange is one of four potential debutants in England's 23-strong squad for the World Cup.
fullText:
Australia-born Jasmin Strange is one of four potential debutants in England's 23-strong squad for the World Cup.

Sydney Roosters second-row forward Strange, who is set to play in Sunday's NRLW Grand Final against Brisbane Broncos, has committed herself to England, for whom she qualifies through her mother Adele.

The 23-year-old is the daughter of Roosters women's head coach John Strange, who played for Featherstone in the 1990s.

Strange is joined by three uncapped players - Leeds Rhinos' Connie Boyd, Hope Millard of Canterbury Bulldogs, and Wigan Warriors' Lucie Sams.

In addition to Strange and Millard, whose father Shane was a forward for Widnes, Leeds and Wigan, three other NRLW players have made the squad - including dual code international Fran Goldthorp, who last played rugby league for her country at the most recent World Cup in 2022.

Newcastle Knights' Georgia Roche and Hollie-Mae Dodd of Canberra Raiders have also been included.

Strange's inclusion as a heritage player - one who qualifies through parentage - comes after eligibility rules were relaxed this year.

An International Rugby League ruling means that players can now represent more than one of the three tier one nations - Australia, New Zealand and England.

That led to speculation that head coach Stu Barrow might call on more heritage players with NRLW experience - such as Roosters playmaker Jocelyn Kelleher, Bulldogs half-back Tayla Preston and Wests Tigers full-back Caitlin Turnbull.

But Barrow has said he wants to give homegrown players an opportunity to develop.

All three Woman of Steel nominees - Jenna Foubister, Eva Hunter and Megan Williams - have been selected, along with six of their Wigan team-mates. Grand Final winners York Valkyrie have one player in the squad in forward Liv Wood.

Loose forward Jodie Cunningham, who will retire after the World Cup, is selected along with St Helens team-mate Vicky Whitfield, who will be competing at her fourth World Cup.

Barrow said: "Narrowing our squad from 40 players to a final 23 has involved some difficult decisions, but we believe we have the right balance of experience and youth to compete on the world stage.

"It's also an exciting moment for the programme with the inclusion of Australian-based heritage players for the first time."

This year's men's, women's and wheelchair World Cups will run concurrently, with England competing in all three. The wheelchair squad was announced last week, while the men's squad will be confirmed on 5 October.

The tournaments are being staged largely in Australia, with Papua New Guinea's men and women each playing two pool matches in their own country, and their New Zealand counterparts playing one.

England face three group matches - beginning in Perth against Wales on 17 October and Australia on 24 October, before facing Samoa in Wollongong on 30 October.

The top two sides in England's four-team group will go through to the semi-finals on 7 and 8 November, with the final on 15 November.

title: Newcastle agree delay to Fineanganofo arrival
description: Free-scoring All Blacks wing Fehi Fineanganofo convinces Newcastle Red Bulls to delay his arrival on Tyneside so he can chase his dream of playing at the Rugby World Cup.
fullText:
Free-scoring All Blacks wing Fehi Fineanganofo has convinced Newcastle Red Bulls to delay his arrival on Tyneside so he can chase his dream of playing at the Rugby World Cup.

It was originally announced back in January that the 24-year-old had agreed a two-year deal with Newcastle, beginning at the start of the current campaign.

However, Fineanganofo's exceptional form with the Wellington-based Hurricanes in Super Rugby then propelled him into Test reckoning.

He made his New Zealand debut against France in July.

Under All Blacks selection rules, a move overseas this year would have put Fineanganofo's emerging international career on ice and ruled him out of contention for the Rugby World Cup, which begins in October 2027.

Newcastle have therefore allowed Fineanganofo to stay with the Hurricanes, for whom he broke the record for the most tries in a single Super Rugby campaign this year, for an extra season.

His Newcastle deal is still for two campaigns, but now covers the 2027-28 and 2028-29 seasons instead.

"I'm really grateful to Newcastle Red Bulls for the support and understanding they've shown me," said Fineanganofo.

"The opportunity to stay in New Zealand and push for selection for the Rugby World Cup means a huge amount, and I'm fully committed to joining the club after the tournament and giving everything I can to the team."

Newcastle's sporting general manager Neil McIlroy said: "We are fully supportive of Fehi's desire to represent his country at Rugby World Cup 2027, which marries with our own philosophy of aiming high and enabling our athletes to achieve their ambitions.

"Fehi's arrival in 2027, with additional international experience that will only add to his already devastating qualities as a top-class winger, is another statement of intent around where this club is going."

The compromise ends long-running uncertainty about Fineanganofo's future.

In June, New Zealand Rugby denied they were attempting to put together a deal to get Fineanganofo out of his Newcastle contract.

Just a few weeks ago, Red Bulls' head coach Dan McFarland said he expected Fineanganofo to arrive in November and play in the current campaign.

His side began the Prem season with former Ulster man Werner Kok, signed in June as doubts over Fineanganofo's move increased, and 35-year-old Christian Wade as their first-choice wings.

McIlroy kept open the possibility of adding to the club's options in that position.

"We are more than happy with the quality and depth that our existing squad possesses, but may yet choose to add to the outside back position if a player of the required standard becomes available," he said.

Newcastle lost 59-26 away to defending champions Northampton on Friday in their league opener, and will take on Leicester at home on Saturday.

fullText:
The U.S. ambassador to China said Trump offered to sell arms to China.

Trump administration officials said on Monday that the United States has no plans to sell weapons to China after U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue indicated during a televised interview that President Donald Trump offered a weapons deal to China's Xi Jinping during a high-profile summit last week.

"President Trump continues to say, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,'" Perdue said Sunday during an appearance on Fox News. "He actually asked President Xi would he like to buy some at one point."

Perdue did not provide further details about the offer, and he did not reveal Xi's response.

A U.S. official denied there were plans to sell weapons to China.

"The U.S. government has no plans to sell weapons to China," the official said to ABC News on Monday.

The State Department also denied a potential sale, saying in a statement to ABC News that "U.S. law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China."

Asked about Perdue's comments in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump said he "didn't discuss it" with Xi, suggesting he meant Taiwan instead of China.

"I never heard of that one. I'm going to have to ask him. You mean we're going to sell? Now they'd probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than them. So maybe it's a good idea. Yeah, but, we didn't discuss it," Trump said, later adding "I think he probably was talking about Taiwan."

A U.S. weapons sale offer to China would be extraordinary, as China is viewed as the primary strategic and economic competitor of the U.S. and is designated as a foreign adversary. The U.S. has placed extensive economic sanctions on China, including economic restrictions, investment bans and contract limits on companies, groups and schools tied to the Chinese military.

The two geopolitical rivals are also competing in the race to develop advanced artificial intelligence and have opposing views over Taiwanese sovereignty.

And in recent weeks, Beijing has come under scrutiny for allegedly providing another U.S. adversary -- Iran -- with satellite imagery in their ongoing conflict with the U.S. and other regional allies.

title: Yesterday sucked... I'll be back, says Cleary
description: Nathan Cleary responds to the horrific injury that has ruled him out of the Rugby League World Cup by promising "I'll be back."
fullText:
Nathan Cleary has responded to the horrific ankle injury that has ruled him out of the Rugby League World Cup by declaring "I'll be back."

The Australia great, 28, will miss the tournament in his home country after suffering a compound fracture and dislocation to his left ankle while playing for Penrith Panthers in their NRL play-off defeat by Newcastle Knights on Sunday.

Half-back Cleary - who helped Australia win the World Cup in Manchester four years ago - needed emergency surgery in hospital after being injured in a tackle by Phoenix Crossland.

Knights hooker Crossland was sent off for a 'hip-drop' tackle - which the NRL outlawed in 2020.

A hip-drop tackle is committed when a defender grabs the runner with both hands or wraps them with both arms, and then swivels or drops the hips or lower body, landing on and trapping the opponent's leg below the knees.

"Surgery done... Thank you so much to everyone that has reached out, the support has been unbelievable," Cleary posted on Instagram.

"Yesterday sucked but it's all part of the journey and it's made me even more grateful for the people I have around me. I'll be back."

Cleary had started Sunday's match on the bench because he was already carrying an injury to his right foot, which had a broken bone.

His father Ivan, the Panthers' head coach, said afterwards that his son would have surgery on both feet.

"I think that's why I was even more emotional on what happened to him, how hard he worked and what he put himself through to get himself to play today," the coach said.

Crossland was referred to the NRL Judiciary over the tackle, and is likely to receive a lengthy ban which would not only rule him out of Sunday's NRL Grand Final, in which Newcastle face Sydney Roosters, but may also affect his availability for New Zealand during the World Cup.

Australia will face New Zealand in the opening match of the World Cup in Sydney on 15 October (10:05 BST). The two teams are also favourites to face each other in the final, in Brisbane on 15 November (08:35 GMT).

title: Trump asked China's Xi if he wants to buy U.S. arms, ambassador says
description: — President Donald Trump has justified the pending U.S. arms sale to Taiwan to Chinese President Xi Jinping by downplaying it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world — even asking Xi if he’d be in the market for U.S. arms, Trump’s ambassador to China said on Sunday.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has justified the pending U.S. arms sale to Taiwan to Chinese President Xi Jinping by downplaying it as just one of many sales Washington makes around the world — even asking Xi if he'd be in the market for U.S. arms, Trump's ambassador to China said on Sunday.

David Perdue said Trump raised the prospect of the arms sales from the U.S. to its ascendant geopolitical rival, an unlikely offer that if consummated would upend generations of U.S. policy toward China and Taiwan and potentially expose U.S. technology to a potential foe. Perdue, speaking to Shannon Bream on "Fox News Sunday" days after Trump hosted Xi for a state visit in Washington, didn't specify when the offer was made.

Bream had cited concerns from Republican and Democratic lawmakers over delayed aid packages and weapons orders to Taiwan, the self-ruled democracy, to defend itself from China's threat to invade the island. Bream asked if the U.S. is denying arms to Taiwan to appease the Chinese president, who visited Trump last week.

Perdue pushed back on the suggestion, stating that Trump "is as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody" and has sold it plenty of weapons. Perdue also said Trump and Xi continue to talk about future U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan.

"But President Trump continues to say, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,'" Perdue said. "He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point."

The U.S. is bound by its own laws to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. While not recognizing Taiwan as a country, the U.S. is the island's strongest informal backer and arms provider. But multiple U.S. leaders have left ambiguous whether they would commit military force to defend the U.S. ally should China invade.

China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a previous summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a "very good negotiating chip" with China.

In their private talks at the White House last week, Xi pressed Trump to oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did not confirm Perdue's remarks when asked about the matter on Monday. But he told reporters that China has always strengthened its national defense capabilities based on its needs, and is committed to maintaining world peace and stability.

title: Carlos Alcaraz wants to make one ‘request’ to tennis chiefs after what happened at the Laver Cup

fullText:
Carlos Alcaraz played another very important role for Team Europe as they reclaimed the Laver Cup from Team World.

Alcaraz finished the tournament with a 100% record, winning his one singles match and one doubles match in London. He earned one point for a doubles win with Jakub Mensik against Alexander Bublik and Taylor Fritz, and two points for a singles win over Fritz. The Spaniard was scheduled to play against Alex de Minaur on day three of three, but Alexander Zverev claimed the Laver Cup title for the hosts before then.

The winning Laver Cup team gathered for a press conference after the victory, where both Mensik and Alcaraz were tasked with discussing the speed of the courts at the event. The O2 arena in London played host to the hard-court, indoor ATP event, where no ranking points are available, but matches count towards head-to-head records.

Told the conditions looked slow and difficult to play in, Mensik and Alcaraz were asked for their opinions on the matter. It was also suggested to the pair that indoor tennis allows players to attack more, with the duo asked what it was really like and if they think it should be different in the future.

Mensik replied: "Well, yeah, obviously, especially me or I guess all of us, we felt like the conditions were pretty slow, which, yeah, compared to the other tournaments, it's one of the probably slowest surfaces that I have played on this year, like as far as hard courts are here.

"So yeah, I mean, it was really tough for me to get used to it, to get the rhythm. Especially for me, my game is a lot about the serve and heavy groundstrokes. It's even more difficult for me to finish the ball. So, you know, the trend of this, I didn't really know where it's going, but obviously with the combination of the balls, which I consider them that they were not that good, as well, it was super slow."

And Alcaraz commented: "I mean, for me, I don't mind slow courts. You know, especially with my serve, it's not the biggest one. No, but yeah, in terms of, you know, I mean, I have been talking with Yannick [Noah], the team, how the tennis has improved over the years, how fast it was the courts back then. And now, you know, it's getting slower, but I think it's not about the courts. It is about the balls, I would say.

"You know, we can see during a lot of tournaments how the balls' reaction from the court is totally different. The ball becomes super big, and it's a totally different game when it's new balls. We play two or three games with those balls, you have to adapt yourself the best you can.

"I don't know where if they're going to change it or not, but what I request is that they have to see the best ball possible for the courts are made, the tournaments we're going to play. I think that's a really important thing to know. But, you know, who knows? What I can say is I'm trying to adapt myself and the game the best I can in the tournament that I go."

It remains to be seen whether or not Alcaraz's request will be granted, but he clearly isn't the only player having an issue with the balls being used. But he is one of many top players who must quickly move on amid the busy ATP calendar, where there is very little time to try and make a successful switch from tournament to tournament and court to court.

That is a skill Alcaraz has mastered throughout his glittering career so far, which takes him to Tokyo next. Alcaraz loves the Laver Cup, but he now returns to more competitive action at the Japan Open, where he is the defending champion.

title: McNulty first US world road race winner in 33 years

fullText:
Brandon McNulty became the first American winner of the men's road race world title in 33 years with a stunning victory in Montreal.

The 28-year-old put his hands on his head in disbelief as he crossed the line 13 seconds clear of the chasing pack, completing the gruelling 273.4km course in six hours and 17 minutes.

Australian Michael Matthews was second, with former winner Mathieu van der Poel, of the Netherlands, in third.

The last American winner of the race was Lance Armstrong in 1993.

"Until the last 800m I didn't believe, I was so tired," said McNulty.

"I'm at a loss for words. I knew something could happen but it would take a miracle and I guess today a miracle happened".

He launched an attack going into the final 30km and was 50 seconds clear going into the last lap.

McNulty visibly began to tire on the final climb and his lead was cut to just 10 seconds, but the chasing pack were unable to reel him in.

Britain's Tom Pidcock finished seventh, with Ireland's Ben Healy 10th and Remco Evenepoel of Belgium in 12th place.

Even without injured riding legend Tadej Pogacar, Montreal 2026 was still full of favourites who were expected to dictate the shape of this monumentally long race.

Van der poel, Evenepoel, Wout van Aert, Paul Seixas and Pidcock were all there, all animating and pushing to breakaway from one another under gradually yellowing Canadian maples.

But timing, not power or race craft, proved crucial.

Such was the distance all attacked far too early, and it was McNulty - a time triallist and domestique to Pogacar by trade - who took off and emptied himself.

The unassuming and, at times, seemingly timid American is a very popular winner of what was unquestionably one of the best races of a long season.

fullText:
To visit Bab el-Mandeb is to understand that old adage about looks being deceiving. For this humble fishing village in Yemen, a tumbledown grouping of barely-there huts nestled between the water and an imposing mountain range, stands sentinel over one of the world's most vital waterways.

The village shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow passageway connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea that's become another flash point in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

"You hear so much about Bab el-Mandeb, you'd think we would be like New York, with skyscrapers and money," said Saleh, a 58-year-old resident who, like all people interviewed here, refused to give their full name to avoid reprisals.

"So many ships pass near here. If the Yemeni government knew how to invest in it, we would be rich. We should be bringing in billions of dollars. Instead, look around you," he said, pausing as his gaze took in the sorry-looking boats haphazardly laid on the beach.

Saleh was interviewed in January, when Bab el-Mandeb was thrust into the power struggle between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the friendly-but-occasionally-fractious backers of Yemen's internationally recognized government.

That war of wills ended with the Emirates ceding control of Bab el-Mandeb — along with the nearby island of Perim, where the Emirates had built a drone airbase — to Saudi Arabia.

But this month, control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait switched once more, when the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, ousted government forces from the waterway in a blitzkrieg in which they seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast.

The move grants the Houthis a valuable foothold in controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ribbon of Red Sea — known as the "Gate of Tears" for the dangers involving its navigation — between Yemen's coast and Djibouti and Eritrea.

About 7% of global energy supplies and around 12% to 15% of all global shipping transit the strait. And in taking Perim Island, which lies in the middle the Red Sea at the strait's narrowest point (a mere 12½ miles), the Houthis could harass ships with ease.

"We don't need a drone or a missile," one Houthi commander bragged in a social media video posted from the island. Instead, he added, all they had to do was place a few artillery units on Perim's coast and they would be able to strike any ship crossing the strait.

The impact of any movement disruption through Bab el-Mandeb wouldn't be limited to already skittish energy markets: To enter the Suez Canal's southern entrance, ships must first transit through Bab el-Mandeb, meaning any trouble in the passageway would force freighters to circumnavigate the African continent — adding anywhere from 12 to 21 days to voyages and spiking fuel costs.

A shipping disaster in 2021 shows how blocking the strait — and thus severing a link to the Mediterranean Sea — could harm global commerce. A container ship in the Suez Canal ran aground and blocked the waterway for six days, delaying the delivery of billions of dollars of goods.

More recently, the Houthis sealed off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in 2023 to coerce Israel into stopping its campaign in Gaza; that pushed the U.S. to attack the Houthis, before the Trump administration agreed to a ceasefire of its own with the group.

These days, the Houthi advance comes at a particularly fraught moment, one in which Bab el-Mandeb has taken on outsize importance. With the Israeli-U.S. war on Iran prompting Tehran to seal the Strait of Hormuz — cutting off the world's most important energy passageway — Persian Gulf oil powerhouses have been forced to divert crude exports to alternatives, including Bab el-Mandeb.

That's especially true for Saudi Arabia, which turned to its East-West pipeline and exports through the Red Sea to sidestep the trouble in Hormuz. But it's also the most vulnerable to the Houthi threat.

The Houthis have a long-running animus against the Saudis, which began in 2015, months after the Houthis overran the Yemeni capital of Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia, spooked about the notion of an Iranian ally on its border, led a coalition — with U.S. backing — to dislodge them. It started a blockade and a devastating air campaign that persisted until a 2022 truce.

But in July, the ceasefire broke after the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking Sanaa's airport in what appeared to be an attempt to stop Iranian flights from landing there. The Houthis began attacking Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and declared a naval blockade against the kingdom.

The rebels' land grab this month stunned Saudi Arabia, which failed to launch airstrikes and stanch the rout of its allied forces from the coast. Saudi leaders reportedly reached out to President Trump to push the rebels back, but he appears disinclined to help.

Still, on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, "We have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement." He did not elaborate on what U.S. support that would entail.

On Thursday, Saudi Arabia said its defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif, a manufacturing center, and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea. It responded with hundreds of strikes on the Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen.

For their part, the Houthis insist they have no plans to attack shipping on the Red Sea and that their blockade applies only to Saudi Arabia — a move calculated to prevent the rise of an international effort to dislodge them.

"They don't want to attract international military operations," said Mohammad al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory.

"They realize that when you do things in the Red Sea, you create panic in the world."

But leaders in the internationally recognized Yemeni government say the Houthis are not to be trusted.

"The Houthi militias' use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy," Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.

He added that protecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the responsibility of "every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation."

In the meantime, the Houthis have been consolidating their gains on Yemen's coast, Basha said, setting up checkpoints and bringing loyalists to administer the regions now under their control.

In taking the coastal areas around Bab el-Mandeb village, they reap the benefit of Emirati investment, manifested in kilometers of paved highways that stand in stark contrast to much of Yemen's road network. They also gain control of several airbases in the area, most crucially on Perim, where the Emirates spent years ferrying construction supplies to build out a roughly 6,000-foot runway along with three hangars.

Although such a runway could not be used by larger bombers, it still can accommodate attack and surveillance aircraft. Another area of the island, which lies roughly two miles off of Yemen's coast, has what appears to be a helicopter landing area.

One resident in Bab el-Mandeb village said much of that construction was done by the Emirates, whose contractors would ferry Southeast Asian construction workers to the island and provide them with food. It also built roughly 100 structures for Perim's residents.

Government forces have since overcome their initial disarray and stopped further Houthi advances. But Basha warned any attempt to push out the Houthis from the coast will be difficult, especially with the group's advances in manufacturing and fielding drones and ballistic missiles, not to mention the divisions and competing loyalties plaguing Yemeni government forces.

"It's an uphill battle," he said.

"You have a divided command-and-control; a divided Yemen; a divided society; a divided geography; and these divisions empower the Houthis."

title: The largest privately owned laser just turned on
description: Fusion startup Xcimer fired up the world's largest privately owned laser.
fullText:
Fusion startup Xcimer Energy on Wednesday flipped the switch on its Phoenix laser system, which the company says is the largest privately owned example in the world.

Xcimer’s approach to fusion power is modeled after the National Ignition Facility (NIF), which proved in December 2022 that a controlled fusion reaction could release more power than required to ignite it.

The NIF trained 192 laser beams on a fuel target smaller than a pencil eraser. The energy from the lasers hit the gold target. As the lasers obliterate the gold target, their energy is converted into X-rays, which are focused on the fuel pellet inside, compressing it until atoms in the fuel fuse and release energy.

The company is betting that more powerful, less complex lasers will help turn NIF’s concept for fusion power into something more profitable.

Xcimer’s plans for a fusion power plant call for two lasers capable of firing in microsecond-long pulses. Light from those pulses will be fed through a compression system, of sorts, which will delivers the lasers’ energy to the fuel target in nanoseconds. The quicker the fuel is compressed, the more likely it is to generate usable fusion reactions.

Phoenix is a step toward an eventual power plant. The system uses excimer amplification, similar to those used in semiconductor manufacturing but significantly more powerful. At full strength, the krypton-fluoride laser generates over 1 kilojoule of energy, Xcimer told TechCrunch, and its core is 38 meters long.

While that may be the most powerful privately owned laser, it’s still a fraction of what the company says it will need for a commercial power plant, which could exceed 12 megajoules.

Xcimer hopes to complete a prototype in 2028 before working on a larger system that it hopes will produce at least as much power as it consumes. Sometime in the mid-2030s, it is planning to build its first commercial-scale power plant.
