title: NI qualifying for World Cup 'surreal' - O'Hanlon
description: Northern Ireland netball vice-captain Caroline O'Hanlon says "not many outside of our camp expected us to qualify" after the booked their spot in the 2027 World Cup in Australia.
fullText:
Northern Ireland netball vice-captain Caroline O'Hanlon said "not many outside of our camp expected us to qualify" after the side booked their spot for the 2027 World Cup in Australia.

Sheonah Forbes' side secured their place in Sydney after beating Wales and the Republic of Ireland during their impressive qualifying campaign in East Kilbride.

It will be the first World Cup for Northern Ireland since 2019, after they missed out on the 2023 edition in Cape Town.

"There wouldn't have been many outside of our camp who expected us to qualify," O'Hanlon told BBC Sport NI.

"It's so exciting, even since Friday, we've been inundated with well wishes and messages from home and people watching the games on BBC. It's been brilliant to have that exposure.

"It just seems surreal. We've been training away and we knew we had that potential, but obviously potential is one thing, getting it over the lines is a different thing and I am so proud of the group that we were able to get it over the line."

World-ranked number 15 Northern Ireland's emphatic 73-50 victory over Republic of Ireland in their final qualifier was not enough to secure one of the two qualification spots automatically.

However, Scotland's narrow win over Wales in Sunday's later game booked both teams spots with Wales, who are ranked ninth in the world, missing out.

"It was a real rollercoaster of a day," O'Hanlon continued.

"Obviously we started out with a hard-fought win against the Republic of Ireland, but we knew that we were still relying on Scotland.

"That match was just up and down the whole way through, so we were nerve-wrecked watching that. Just sitting in the stands, not being able to control anything, was nerve-wracking."

O'Hanlon was captain of the side when they finished 10th in the World Cup seven years ago.

But, now, the 31-year-old said the squad will head to Sydney with ambitions of competing for results rather than simply gaining experience.

"The last one we were at was in Liverpool and there was a lot of home support, but Sydney is the home of netball at the minute," O'Hanlon added.

"Sydney is the centre of the best league in the world. It'll be a brilliant spectacle and it's just class to be a part of it.

"The group will be going into the games not just to experience, not just to learn, but to actually go on and compete and try to win games and get results. That's the next step for us really."

title: Fernandes, Gakpo & Dorgu join international break's injury list
description: Bruno Fernandes, Cody Gakpo and Patrick Dorgu all join the international break's high-profile injury list after suffering issues that have curtailed their involvement in Nations League matches.
fullText:
Bruno Fernandes, Cody Gakpo and Patrick Dorgu have all joined the international break's high-profile injury list after suffering issues that have curtailed their involvement in Nations League matches.

After playing in Portugal's win over Wales on Thursday, Manchester United captain Fernandes was not in the squad for Sunday's fixture against Norway.

Prior to the match boss Jorge Jesus revealed, external Fernandes had "played through the pain" against Wales and "wasn't his usual self".

"He played with an injury he brought from Manchester United," he said. "He really wanted to play against Wales."

Meanwhile, both Fernandes' United team-mate Dorgu and Liverpool striker Gakpo suffered injuries during games for their respective countries on Sunday.

Gakpo had to go off just 16 minutes into the Netherlands' 2-1 win against Serbia, grimacing and holding the lower part of his right leg.

He has started the season well for Liverpool with two goals and four assists in six appearances across all competitions.

Dorgu, meanwhile, lasted 30 minutes before he limped off in Denmark's 2-0 win against Wales.

The first international break of the 2026-27 men's football season is lasting a week longer than it usually does, with the traditional October break now scrapped.

There is now a three-week gap for international fixtures across late September and early October, where countries will play four international matches instead of two.

Injured Isak returns to Liverpool from Sweden duty

Why will September international break last three weeks?

Gakpo's injury adds to Liverpool's woes after Alexander Isak withdrew from Sweden duty with a minor thigh injury.

The striker played the full 90 minutes and scored a goal in his side's 2-1 win on Friday over Romania in the Nations League.

However, he will not be involved in Sweden's remaining three matches in this international break and assessed by his club's medical staff.

On Thursday, Arsenal forward Kai Havertz and Sunderland's Brian Brobbey both went off injured in the same game as the Netherlands drew with Germany.

German Havertz was caught on the knee by a high boot from Quinten Timber in Amsterdam and had to be replaced.

Netherlands forward Brobbey - off the back off a hat-trick in Sunderland's 5-3 Premier League defeat by Manchester City - then appeared to suffer a muscle injury.

A further blow for Sunderland on this international break came as Dan Ballard suffered a hamstring injury late in Northern Ireland's 1-0 win over Georgia on Friday.

Boss Michael O'Neill has confirmed the injury will rule him out of the national team's remaining fixtures in this international break.

It is not just Premier League teams who are being impacted by injuries to their players while on international duty.

Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe has been ruled out for at least two weeks after injuring his knee while scoring the winner in Zinedine Zidane's first game in charge of France.

He scored a record-extending 67th goal from Michael Olise's pass to sink Turkey, but he was limping immediately and had to be replaced five minutes later.

Meanwhile, Bayern Munich's Jamal Musiala suffered a muscle injury during the warm-up for the game against the Netherlands and had to withdraw.

title: England win series as Banton delivers on potential
description: Tom Banton delivers on all of his potential by crashing a brilliant first international century as England wrapped up their summer with an ODI series win over Sri Lanka.
fullText:
Third Metro Bank one-day international, Kia Oval

England 355-7 (50 overs): Banton 126, Brook 77, Cox 76

Sri Lanka 132 (29.1 overs): Kusal 35; Dawson 3-26

Tom Banton delivered on all of his potential by crashing a brilliant first international century as England wrapped up their summer with an ODI series win over Sri Lanka.

The 27-year-old right-hander was once the rising star of English cricket when handed a debut in 2019 but afterwards fell out of love with the game after losing his way.

After reaching his hundred in 95 balls in the third one-day international at The Oval, he stood with arms wide and looked to the sky - all of that disappointment seemingly behind him.

"My fiance, Lilly, was here and all of her family," Banton said.

"Unfortunately, my mum, dad and brother weren't here because whenever my mum seems to come I don't do that well.

"Bless her, she is not banned from coming, but she avoids coming now."

The opener went on to make 126 from 105 deliveries, perfectly countering tricky early conditions - conditions in which Joe Root struggled uncharacteristically for 18 from 37 balls - and going on to share an increasingly aggressive stand of 150 in 117 balls with captain Harry Brook.

"To score a hundred for England is just the best feeling on earth," Banton said. "I don't think anything is going to beat it."

Brook made 77 and Jordan Cox, picked in the place of the injured Jos Buttler, added a 52-ball 76 to lift England to 355-7.

That always appeared a match-winning total on a surface offering bounce for the pace bowlers and turn for the spinners.

Sri Lanka crumbled to 132 all out in 29.1 overs, giving England a 223-run win and their biggest ODI victory against the tourists.

It meant England signed off their summer, one that included off-field issues, the end of Bazball, Ben Stokes' retirement and Root's surprise return as Test skipper, with a fifth successive series win amid the madness across formats.

Banton blasts England to series win

England thrash Sri Lanka by 223 runs to win ODI series - reaction, analysis & clips

Banton's success is heartwarming. When, fresh out of Second XI cricket, he made his debut as a 20-year-old in 2019 he was seen as England's next big thing.

He was in the same England Under-19 team as Brook but, rather than the Yorkshireman who is now captain, it was the Somerset product who was given the opportunity when Eoin Morgan's World Cup-winning side needed a fresh face on its journey forward.

Tougher times followed, resulting in almost five years out of the 50-over side and only occasional T20 appearances.

During that time Kevin Pietersen, now an England mentor, said Banton "has all the talent but, at the moment, he is wasting it".

It was comparisons to Pietersen which Banton struggled with. Last week, Banton said remains "in awe" of the iconic England batter.

With thrilling reverse sweeps here, he showed the invention that drew those comparisons. He was also vicious on the pull, hit classically through the covers and, when Ben Duckett was bowled in the second over and Root faced 13 dot balls in a row, did not panic.

When he walked off he turned and raised his bat amid a standing ovation from The Oval crowd – as Pietersen famously did 21 years ago.

Banton only has the opportunity as opener here because of Jacob Bethell's injury.

He may find himself out of the XI when England begin a tri-series in Pakistan - a series that also involves Sri Lanka - on 20 October.

The tourists, impressive in setting up this decider on Thursday, were poor here. They had already dropped Root before he was dismissed and wicketkeeper and captain Kusal Mendis spilled a thick edge when Brook had seven.

Afterwards the England captain started slowly but he kicked it into life from a position of 108-2 after 25 overs.

Also encouraging was the performance of Cox, whose knock also built on a slow start and followed an impressive run in the Test side against Pakistan.

Sonny Baker, recalled for his second ODI in place of Josh Tongue, nicked off Pathum Nissanka with a quick, swinging and rising delivery two balls into the second over, after which Sri Lanka did not recover. Left-arm spinner Liam Dawson also repaid the faith for his inclusion over Rehan Ahmed with figures of 3-26.

This summer has provided so many issues for England, including the end of Brendon McCullum's reign as Test coach.

Still his ODI side now has momentum - a third series win a row - as it builds towards next year's World Cup. Series in Pakistan, Australia and South Africa are to come this winter.

Sunday morning, Air Force One made its approach in the Chicagoland area and did a flyover at Medinah Country Club.

After touching down, Trump's motorcade made its way to Medinah, host of the 16th Presidents Cup.

Trump spoke briefly with reporters after landing in Chicago, saying, “You'll be seeing the best players, the best golfers anywhere in the world. It's going to be great. I think for those of you that don't play, you'll get it," he said ahead of his arrival to Medinah.

Fans were alerted 12 hours prior to expect delays and enhanced security measures and additional restrictions.

Gates opened at 8 a.m. and fans quickly filled the first tee, though, in anticipation of an American comeback. The U.S. started the final day down 10½ to 7½.

Trump walked out to the trophy stand at the first tee at Medinah to loud cheers and some lesser scattered boos that were drowned out by "U-S-A!" chants. He was then introduced by the CEO of the PGA Tour, Brian Rolapp.

Golfweek reported Saturday that Trump had requested to speak at the first tee for 15 minutes before the start of play but that didn't occur. Instead, Trump made some brief remarks, joking he was not brave enough to subject the crowd to a speech, then jabbed at the "fake news media", whom he joked would report he received a poor reception, before posing for pictures.

A few fans chanted out "four more years" in the stands behind him before Trump smiled and waved to the crowd a few more times, then departed.

Trump then hung out on the first tee, shaking hands with each U.S. player ahead of their opening tee shots.

title: Injured Assefa narrowly misses world record in Berlin
description: Ethiopian runner Tigst Assefa wins the Berlin Marathon but narrowly misses out on breaking the women's world record because of injury.
fullText:
An injured Tigst Assefa hobbled over the line at the Berlin Marathon on Sunday after looking set to smash the women's world record.

The Ethiopian still won with the third-fastest time in history in two hours 11 minutes four seconds.

But the 29-year-old, a silver medallist at the Paris Olympics two years ago, had been cruising to a new record before fading in the final stages.

Kenyan athlete Ruth Chepngetich's time of 2:09:56, set at the 2024 Chicago Marathon, remains the world record time, though that result is overshadowed by the three-year doping ban she received in 2025.

Assefa, the 2026 London Marathon winner, started rapidly and led the field by a minute at the 15km mark. She was ahead of the record pace at 35km and is a renowned fast finisher - but began to suffer clear discomfort and her pace slowed.

However she still broke the Berlin course record of 2:11:53 that she set in 2023 - which was also her previous personal best.

In addition, she improved on her time of 2:15:41 at the London Marathon earlier this year.

"We have to bow our heads to this performance. She was on a world record course for most of the race but then something happened to her tendon," said race director Mark Milde.

"To finish like this, I've never seen something like this. The pain is hard to imagine.

"With a heavy heart, we saw her set a course record, but it could have been a lot more."

The top five finishers were all from Ethiopia, with Bedatu Hirpa second and Dera Dida third.

Guye Adola - another Ethiopian - won the men's race with a time of 2:02:50.

title: Parsons becomes record try scorer as Ireland beat Japan

fullText:
The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a Silicon Valley mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “System Error: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”.

When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”

The technos were onto something. Silicon Valley’s power players have just been blindsided by democracy, which has slammed into their program to transform the world with artificial intelligence. A cabal that never doubted the greatness of their ambitions unexpectedly finds their project in the hot seat, forcing them into the unusual position of having to persuade the great unwashed of the merits of their endeavor. So far, the public is not buying. And for all their blindingly high IQs and their massively endowed wallets, Silicon Valley’s greats don’t quite know what to do.

Everyday Americans are up in arms against the AI datacenters sprouting across their communities. Villages, counties, cities and states are imposing moratoria and bans on further development. While the backlash has largely focused on stopping the proliferation of sprawling sites packed with energy-guzzling computer servers, the revolt is not merely nimby opposition to local development.

Public opinion has also turned decidedly sour on the AI project that has called these datacenters into being. Some 73% of Americans think the costs of datacenters outweigh the benefits, according to a survey by the Marquette University Law School. The same survey found that 70% of Americans think that AI is bad for society.

Americans were not always this down on the tech. In 2021, only 37% declared themselves more concerned than excited about the technology, according to surveys by the Pew Research Center. But the share has climbed to 52%. Even 55% of young adults – usually the most excited cohort – have soured on it. And this is not a partisan fear. Democrats and Republicans alike are vastly more concerned than excited. Interestingly, Americans are generally more mistrustful of the technology than people in other countries.

This surely has something to do with the terrifying announcements that have come out of Silicon Valley recently. A widely shared belief that there’s at least a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction has, rightly, scared the bejesus out of many and follows repeated statements that artificial intelligence will end all jobs as we know them. Assuming we do avoid an AI apocalypse, vague promises of an AI cure for cancer and a universal basic income or some such to replace wages across the economy sound hollow coming from a clutch of out-of-touch billionaires with questionable moral codes in a country with huge holes in its social safety net.

The political backlash is built on a deeper discomfort, though, beyond fear of the dystopia threatened by the masters of the valley. A fear built in the here and now and fueled by a brooding mistrust in US democracy itself, distrust of a political system that allowed a clutch of weird, sci-fi addled plutocrats to pursue a civilization-threatening project behind people’s backs. As noted Henry Farrell, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, “the push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives.”

People are not wrong about this. As AI ethicist Rumman Chowdhury points out, the dominant narrative out of Silicon Valley, that AI systems are becoming so powerful that nobody – including the companies that developed them – can stop them, is a stratagem to avoid responsibility for whatever harm their products may cause, depriving meat-and-bones humans of any recourse to law.

The popular backlash is unlikely to stop the buildout of datacenters. Donald Trump remains steadfastly on the side of the moguls hoping to build an AI future. In response to the popular backlash, the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to nix the rule that requires states to solicit public input on applications for air pollution permits for industrial facilities like datacenters and the power plants that feed them, which could keep locals in the dark until construction starts.

The sorry truth is that tech’s power does insulate it from small democratic pressure. “If there is one sector in the US that is still globally dominant and profitable, it is tech,” Boston University historian Quinn Slobodian said. “They can be confident that even if there is a change of leadership, the next person will have to dance with them anyway.”

Critically, there is a bipartisan consensus that ensuring the US’s capabilities in artificial intelligence remain ahead of China’s is of paramount importance. Fear of Chinese catch-up is likely to keep driving policy, overriding voters’ concerns about the risks embodied in this new technology.

And yet voters’ rejection of datacenters, the most immediate, concrete expression of the AI project, raises a question about how the technological revolution of our time will deal with intense popular skepticism and navigate democratic governance. It poses a challenge to a technological elite which exhibits nothing but contempt toward democratic rule.

This is not, of course, the first time that some technological revolution brings about societal upheaval without asking for democratic buy-in. The people that brought about America’s transformation from an agricultural society to an industrial powerhouse did not survey farmers about what mechanization would do to their farms. The Luddites of 19th century England would have loved the chance to put approval of the steam-powered loom to a referendum.

But technological change over the last few decades has not delivered the kind of uplift to everyday workers that their ancestors enjoyed as they were displaced from agriculture to join a highly productive industrial labor force. Automation, instead, has flushed workers without a college degree into a low productivity economy where hotel and restaurant workers, nursing home caretakers, janitors and 7-11 cashiers eke out a living on little more than the minimum wage. Americans have earned their skepticism about the wonders of AI.

One must wonder how such a transformative project as the mass deployment of artificial intelligence across society and the economy will navigate today’s democratic political systems. The technological elite’s contempt for the people’s concerns suggests that they hope to somehow bypass popular concerns in pursuit of the AI program. It seems unlikely that a crew of billionaires who dream of building enclaves at sea, outside the legal jurisdiction of any state, will simply accept democratic constraints. The question is what they will do to overcome them.

Until China became a hi-tech powerhouse and proved them wrong, the political class across the liberal market democracies of the West was convinced that capitalism needed democracy to thrive. But the neoliberal project that guided policy across much of the 20th century was largely about putting capitalism beyond democracy’s reach.

The emergence of independent central banks like the Federal Reserve, which is supposed to set interest rates free from political pressure, is perhaps the prime example of this process. The agreements that led to the creation of the World Trade Organization were largely about putting trade policy beyond the reach of domestic politics. Myriad international treaties were similarly designed to protect economic intercourse from democratic challenges, to provide businesses insulation from political agendas and guarantee the political stability they required to invest.

But the neoliberal project was not driven by “a foundational belief that democracy needs to be snuffed out entirely,” noted Slobodian, author of “Globalists” which traces the history of neoliberalism, as well as an explanatory tome on Elon Musk, “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.” It “acknowledged at some basic level the legitimacy of democracy, which needs to be counterbalanced.”

The barons of Silicon Valley are not so forgiving. “The Silicon Valley leadership class has a programmers’ mentality,” said Slobodian. “For them, the messiness of democracy has no function or utility. It is only bad code.”

Peter Thiel, the weirdest of the Silicon Valley billionaires, who can’t but bring up the Antichrist in every conversation, has argued that democracy and liberty are incompatible. Similar strains of thought are also popular with the less idiosyncratic billionaires in the Valley ecosystem. OpenAI’s Sam Altman salivates about an “awesome” future in which human presidents are replaced with an AI that “can go around and talk to every person on Earth, understand their exact preferences at a very deep level, you know, how they think about this issue and that one and how they balance the trade-offs and what they want and then understand all of that and like collectively optimize for the collective preferences of humanity or of citizens of the US.”

The technos’ conflict is not exclusively with democracy. It is with any institution that dares impose constraints on whatever Grand Project they plan to unleash on the world. This could be reconfiguring human interactions by plugging everybody into social media, inventing a new form of money that can evade government control, civilizing space or bringing about a superintelligent Golem.

Musk has no patience for corporate governance tools that may limit what he can do at the helm of his empire. He aspires to be answerable to no one and will organize his companies to that effect. Thiel can’t even countenance competition. It “means no profits for anybody, no meaningful differentiation, and a struggle for survival,” he has fumed. Across the Valley, these thoughts draw from an unshakeable faith in the civilizational, transformative greatness of their endeavor. Technology will solve the world. They will provide the technology. Everybody else, please get out of the way.

There is, however, a historical discontinuity to the story of these masters of the universe: They used to think of themselves as the Good Guys in the liberal democratic fold. Most of them were aligned with the Democratic Party, culturally liberal, empathetic, and willing to accept some modicum of taxation to finance redistribution. Emerging after the collapse of the Soviet block and the end of the Cold War, they saw themselves and their companies as agents of the End of History in Francis Fukuyama’s sense of the word.

Social media–Silicon Valley’s original Grand Project– would overcome the censorship and limits to expression that underpin authoritarian rule, unshackling freedom of expression and opening the floodgates for liberty and democracy. The project sounded so good that the masters of the Valley managed to convince Congress in 1996 to give them a free pass: section 230 of the Telecommunications Act, which said social media companies were not responsible for anything posted on their platforms, based on the dubious argument that they just provided the blackboard but had no say over what was written on it.

Then, the tech moguls’ love affair with democracy went sour. For it turned out that social media could also do a lot of damage. Reports of teen suicides and online bullying bred unease about social media, which built into open mistrust as it became evident that the billionaires at the helm of these technologies knew about the potential perils of their products and yet kept adding features designed to hook users to their screens.

When social media platforms emerged as vectors of misinformation and political manipulation during the 2016 election, the romance between the tech bros and society fractured irretrievably. Founders and their funders who were used to being revered as purveyors of rainbows and puppies, found themselves under harshly unsympathetic scrutiny.

How long will the honeymoon last? Mark Zuckerberg seems excited about the gold chains, the new hairdo and the mixed martial arts. Perhaps his embrace of the Maga-friendly manosphere is genuine. Musk, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Altman all seem comfy in Trump’s squishy embrace. And Trump’s Washington keeps giving Silicon Valley what it wants. The administration is promising to punish European countries who dare fine the US’s hi-tech behemoths. The president has called the power plants built to feed AI datacenters “beautiful”. And he will never do anything to hinder crypto, which is proving so lucrative for him and his family.

Still, the furious backlash against datacenters suggests that Silicon Valley’s Maga-friendly strategy may run out of runway. Their allegiance with Trump, whose popularity ratings are plummeting, may start feeling like an anvil around their neck.

Abdul El-Sayed, the democratic socialist running for the Senate in Michigan, put it this way in a conversation with Jasmine Sun: “This entire industry feels misplaced, and it’s being driven by the interaction between all the worst players. Number one, tech billionaires who are already billionaires, who don’t really need more money but want power. And then VC firms who want to make more money. And then big corporations who want to automate your job. So who wins here? Definitely not the people who live there.”

Silicon Valley may have oodles of money to change the conversation. But it is right to be terrified that this argument may win the day. As Slobodian put it, “the tech barons may not care about democracy, but democracy cares about them.”

Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

fullText:
Two giant pandas sent by China arrived in the United States on Sunday, Beijing's state media said, after a leaders' summit that was heavy on symbolism and light on major breakthroughs.

The pandas' transfer had already been agreed but the departure was announced Thursday during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.

The black-and-white mammals are immensely popular around the world, and China loans them out as part of a "panda diplomacy" programme to foster foreign ties.

Ping Ping and Fu Shuang departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport on a chartered flight at around 3:00 am (1900 GMT on Saturday), state news agency Xinhua reported.

After a 16-hour flight that crossed the international date line, the bears touched down in Atlanta, Georgia shortly before 7:00 am local time (1100 GMT on Sunday), Xinhua said later.

Steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots were prepared to keep the pandas nourished during their flight, Chinese state-run media the Global Times reported.

The Boeing 777 operated by FedEx was the top-tracked aircraft on aviation information platform FlightRadar24 as it neared Alaska, roughly halfway into its journey.

The pandas will be hosted by Zoo Atlanta for the next 10 years.

A farewell ceremony was held for the pair before their departure by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.

Experienced keepers were dispatched by the US side to accompany the duo on their flight, the Global Times reported.

In preparation for their arrival, Zoo Atlanta has renovated its panda facilities and assembled a team of animal caretakers.

It has also ensured a stable and long-term supply of bamboo, grown locally in Atlanta, which has a climate that is very similar to Chengdu.

Zoo Atlanta previously hosted pandas on loan from China for a quarter of a century starting in 1999, but it has not had any since 2024.

Both arrivals were born in 2020. Ping Ping, a male, is now six years old while Fu Shuang, a female, will turn six next month.

Pandas in captivity typically live for around 30 years.

Beijing has sent the furry creatures across the globe for decades as soft-power ambassadors of its diplomatic goodwill.

In 1972, China gifted a pair of pandas to Washington, following US president Richard Nixon's historic visit to the Communist nation.

Beijing recalled two of its pandas from Japan early this year, following a diplomatic spat that began when Japan's prime minister hinted that Tokyo could intervene militarily in the event of any attack on Taiwan.

fullText:
LOURDES, France, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Pope Leo on Sunday urged the Catholic Church to admit its own failings and heal "deep wounds" inflicted within its ranks, hours before he was set to meet victims of child abuse by priests in France.

Leo, addressing crowds stretching out over ‌a large field near the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, said the Church must have the courage to face its past but did not directly ‌reference abuse scandals in France that sparked nationwide shock.

"In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze," the ​first US pope told an estimated 150,000 people gathered in the field on a sunlit day.

Leo is on a whirlwind three-city, four-day visit to France, where he has again urged the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence. He drew around 800,000 people for an outdoor Mass on the Champs-Élysées in Paris on Saturday.

Local Church leaders are hoping he will help repair the Church's standing after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.

In an earlier, ‌closed-door meeting with French bishops on Sunday, Leo did directly ⁠refer to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy," according to a Vatican-provided text.

The pope thanked the bishops for the "courageous measures" he said they had taken to confront the scandals and urged them to buttress their safeguarding efforts and "continue ⁠on the path undertaken, maintaining the greatest vigilance."

VICTIMS SCEPTICAL PAPAL MEETING WILL SPUR ACTION

Leo has previously apologised directly for abuse scandals that have damaged the Church's credibility across the world. On a trip to Spain in June, he told bishops there that they must listen to survivors and offer them reparations.

The pope is due to have a closed-door meeting with seven French victims ​of ​abuse by clergy later on Sunday. Some survivors said they were doubtful the encounter would result ​in quick changes by the Church.

"I am quite sceptical that the ‌pope will solve the issue, at least not immediately," Michèle Le Reun-Gaigné, co-president of an association for survivors in western France, told Reuters.

"Things are moving very slowly," she said. "It isn't going to happen overnight."

Bishop Pierre-Antoine Bozo, the spokesperson for the French bishops, said the pope's desire to have the meeting "shows that we cannot ignore this issue and that it must always remain among our concerns".

LOURDES CONNECTED TO VATICAN SCANDAL

The pope's itinerary in France includes six events in Lourdes, a town in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains that attracts some 3 million pilgrims a year for visits to a shrine to the Virgin Mary and purported healing spring waters.

The site is also connected to a ‌scandal that has dogged the Vatican in recent years. The shrine's facade has a series of ​mosaics by Rev. Marko Rupnik, a prominent religious artist with Vatican ties, who has been accused of ​sexual abuse.

Rupnik, accused by more than 20 women, is not known to ​have commented publicly on the accusations. Five of his alleged victims wrote an open letter to the pope on Thursday, sharply criticising an ‌ongoing Vatican trial of the cleric.

The mosaics, stories tall, have been ​covered for the pope's visit with large, ​muted yellow tarps. Arriving for the Mass on Sunday, Leo was driven in his open-top popemobile near the facade of the shrine and the covered mosaics.

The pope, who on Friday sharply reiterated Catholic opposition to assisted dying initiatives two months after France created a legal right to die for those with incurable ​illnesses, again mentioned the Church's pro-life stance in Lourdes.

Meeting with ‌volunteers who help sick pilgrims hoping to find a miracle in the shrine's waters, Leo urged them to remember the "profound meaning" of healthcare work.

"That ​is to care for a suffering person, not to eliminate that person," said the pope. "Medicine must never become the servant of programmed death!"

title: Alcaraz wins after saving match points as Europe lead Laver Cup

Two-time Wimbledon champion Carlos Alcaraz narrowly avoided back-to-back singles defeats for the first time in 18 months as Team Europe took a 7-5 lead over Team World at the Laver Cup.

The world number three saved two match points before overcoming Taylor Fritz 6-3 4-6 13-11 in a dramatic deciding tie-break at London's O2 Arena.

It was Alcaraz's first singles outing since his late-night quarter-final exit to Ben Shelton at the US Open.

"The drop shot is part of my game," Alcaraz said after sealing victory with a trademark touch.

"In those really close and important moments, I tried to use it because it was a really good weapon for me in this match."

American Fritz, whose only previous victory against the Spaniard came during Team World's triumph in last year's competition, kept errors to a minimum.

However, Alcaraz struck 42 winners to Fritz's 20, bringing an audience that included Roger Federer and Andy Murray to their feet.

Facing match point at 8-9 down in the tie break, Alcaraz fired an ace before leaning on a drop shot to stave off a second. He converted his third match point when Fritz failed to retrieve another delicate drop shot over the net.

Earlier on Saturday, Andre Agassi's Team World had threatened to run away with things.

Alex de Minaur fought back from a set down to shock Alexander Zverev 2-6 7-6 (7-5) 11-9, while American debutant Learner Tien edged Italy's Flavio Cobolli 6-3 2-6 10-7.

Following Alcaraz's singles heroics, Zverev returned to the court alongside Casper Ruud to secure an important 6-4 7-6 (9-7) doubles victory over Alexander Bublik and Brandon Nakashima, keeping Europe ahead going into the final day.

Match wins are worth three points on Sunday, with the first team to reach 13 points lifting the trophy.

Europe are chasing their sixth Laver Cup title, while holders Team World are aiming for their third.

fullText:
Iran stood firm Sunday on its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump's rejection of the proposal that had created some optimism for breaking the Mideast war stalemate.

The waterway is key to the world's energy supply and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was triggered nearly seven months ago with deadly strikes on Iran.

Iran's plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and fulfilling conditions in the ceasefire deal that fell apart months ago.

That agreement, which dissolved during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Araghchi said on Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.

"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights."

But Trump said on Saturday that he rejected the truce deal.

"They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," he told reporters. "They want to make a deal and I think that's fine. I like making a deal too."

Araghchi said on Sunday that the Iranians "saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators".

"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them," the foreign minister added.

Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, to reopen the strait and to launch talks on Iran's nuclear programme.

But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.

Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.

Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

At the UN, Saudi Arabia's Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan complained that the "international community has been absent" and is failing to live up to the responsibility to keep the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab open.

"The kingdom rejects any party's use of these vital passages as a tool for pressure, threat, or harm to the interests of states," he said, stressing the waterways' importance to global energy security.

His Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, told member states that "Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilising this strategically important region."

In New York, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, according to his office, and said: "Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table but, given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States."

Araghchi said at the UN: "Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days."

"The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he added.

Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: "We will not cease punishing the US until Iran's seven conditions are met."

Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran's demands.

title: Who made an uncharacteristic error? England player ratings v Spain
description: England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - here's how BBC Sport rated the Three Lions' players.
fullText:
England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - the Three Lions' first match since this summer's World Cup.

Lamine Yamal gave Spain the lead before goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put England ahead.

Kane then missed a penalty before Alex Baena curled in to level the score, with Mikel Oyarzabal scoring the winner.

Here's how we rated England's players - and you can have your say in the comments at the bottom.

James Trafford: Showed early on his ability to play with the ball at his feet but conceded after just two minutes when Guehi gifted the ball to Lamine Yamal. An important save stopped Torres making it 2-0 in the first half. 6

Jarell Quansah: Continued at right-back after showing what he could do in the position at the World Cup. A physically dominant performance and had a chance to score but headed over. 6

Ezri Konsa: Some shaky moments for Konsa and England's back four but the centre-back regrouped and got better as the game went on. 6

Marc Guehi: An uncharacteristic error gifted the ball - and the opening goal - to Lamine Yamal. 5

Nico O'Reilly: Put in the cross for Kane's goal as England took the lead in the first half. Did a good job of trying to deal with Lamine Yamal. However he gave the ball away for Spain's second goal. 6

Elliot Anderson: Nearly punished for giving the ball away in a dangerous position in the first half but Ferran Torres rolled his shot wide. Anderson and midfield partner Lewis-Skelly took some time to settle in what was a tough night in the middle of the pitch against a Spain side who moved the ball so well. 6

Myles Lewis-Skelly: A first England start in centre midfield for Lewis-Skelly after shining for Arsenal. Given the tough task of trying to shut off the supply to Spain's conductor, Rodri. A solid performance. Replaced after 70 minutes. 6

Jude Bellingham: The Real Madrid midfielder produced another dominant display and was unlucky to be on the losing side. He provided an assist for England's equaliser and won a penalty which Kane hit against the bar after slipping. Stung Simon's palms with a drive in stoppage time. 8

Bukayo Saka: Won a couple of free-kicks around the box and shot over from the edge of the area in the first half. Curled just wide with the score level but a quiet night for the winger. 6

Anthony Gordon: The Barcelona winger scored an excellent goal on the counter-attack. He kept calm when played through on goal by Bellingham when his pace put him clear. A dangerous cross in the first half after England went behind and a threat in behind all night. 8

Harry Kane: Started dropping deep in the first half in search of the ball after England went behind. Scored the second with a deflected header to put England in the lead but missed a penalty when they had the chance to add a third in the second half. 7

James Garner (on 70, Lewis-Skelly): Took on Lewis-Skelly's role of trying to keep Rodri quiet. 6

Morgan Rogers (on 70, Gordon): Did not get much of the ball in his 20 minutes on the pitch. 6

Morgan Gibbs-White (on 83, Saka): Came on and played on the left wing. 6

Calvert-Lewin (on 83, Kane): Not much time to impact the play. 6

Jarrad Branthwaite, (on 89, Guehi): A late change for Guehi in the England backline. No time to make an impression. 6

title: Vollering wins women's road race world title
description: Demi Vollering continues her remarkable season with a thrilling victory in the women's road race in Montreal.
fullText:
Demi Vollering continued her remarkable season with a thrilling victory to win the women's road race world title in Montreal.

The Dutchwoman held off a late challenge from Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney to add another title to her collection, following wins at the Tour de France Femmes, Giro d'Italia Women and World Championships.

The 29-year-old also won a string of one-day classics in the spring, including the Tour of Flanders and Liege-Bastogne-Liege.

"I can still not believe it. I worked so hard towards this goal, and it takes guts to truly believe in it with your whole heart," she said.

Italian Elisa Longo Borghini edged out world time-trial champion Marlen Reusser to take bronze.

Great Britain's Flora Perkins was among 15 riders to crash while speeding downhill early in the race.

Defending champion Magdeleine Vallieres, Mauritius' Kimberley Le Court and Spain's Paula Blasi were also involved and eventually had to withdraw.

Vollering launched her initial attack with about 40km to go only to be reeled in by the chasing pack over the final two laps.

Poland's Niewiadoma-Phinney stayed on her wheel in the closing stages but was beaten to the line, with Vollering claiming victory in four hours 45 minutes nine seconds.

"There were so many moments I thought I went too early," Vollering said. "I didn't dare to turn around and look back because I felt like they were almost on my wheel already.

"I just dared, tried again and never gave up to the finish line."

title: Man United’s financial woes deepen after move that makes a mockery of Ratcliffe’s “world’s most profitable club” claim
description: 1Manchester United’s debt has ballooned even further after the latest move by the club, a report has highlighted.Financial shapeEarlier this week, United released their latest financial results, con...
fullText:
Manchester United's debt has ballooned even further after the latest move by the club, a report has highlighted.

Earlier this week, United released their latest financial results, confirming an annual loss for the seventh successive year. United's combined losses since 2019 now stand at a staggering £444 million.

United posted a net loss of £43 million for 2025/26, which represents a significant increase on the £33 million for the previous 12 months.

Despite record revenue of £677.6 million, up 1.7% year on year, and a major cost-cutting drive under Sir Jim Ratcliffe that has seen hundreds of staff lose their jobs, United's losses have continued.

The Red Devils' wage bill dropped to £301 million, down 3.6% on the previous year, more than £100 million lower than cross-town rivals Manchester City, who were recently found guilty on 114 charges of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

Further details regarding United's financial results are available here.

According to the BBC, more information that was released by the club shows that United borrowed another £90 million since 30 June, piling on further debt.

During the summer transfer window, United secured the signings of Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba for a combined £153 million.

But records show that United forked out £191.7 million on new players this summer. It's unclear where the extra sum was spent.

The BBC explain that United have been contacted for comment.

Simon Stone writes, "Confirmation of the additional borrowing of £90 million was included in a more detailed filing to the New York Stock Exchange on Thursday, following Wednesday's release of their 2025-26 accounts to 30 June, and showed their overall debt was still more than £1 billion."

"United confirmed it made three further drawdowns from its revolving credit limit, on 29 and 31 July and 28 August, totalling £120 million. It then paid back £30 million on 21 September."

The 20-time English champions' overall debt has soared to £1.15 billion. This is made up of the historic debt the Glazers lumped on during their controversial leveraged buyout in 2005 (£578 million), the outstanding amount on the club's revolving credit facility (£200 million) and £375 million in outstanding transfer fees.

It's said that payments for most of United's recent transfers "are due within the next five years."

Certainly, Ratcliffe's assertion that United are now "the most profitable club in the world" rings hollow in light of these latest developments.

title: GB's Potter takes silver at Triathlon World Series
description: Georgia Taylor-Brown finishes second to France's Cassandre Beaugrand at the World Championship Triathlon Series final, with GB team-mates Kate Waugh and Beth Potter in third and fourth respectively.
fullText:
Great Britain's Beth Potter claimed silver at the World Championship Triathlon Series behind Olympic champion Cassandre Beaugrand of France.

The final event of the series took place in Pontevedra, Spain, where Potter needed a win to overhaul Beaugrand in the overall standings.

But she finished fourth, with team-mates Georgia Taylor-Brown and Kate Waugh finishing second and third behind Beaugrand.

Beaugrand won comfortably, completing the 1.5km swim, 40km bike ride and 10km run in one hour 50 minutes 52 seconds, which was over a minute quicker than Taylor-Brown.

Potter, who won the World Series at Pontevedra in 2023, remained in contention at the end of the cycle, but Beaugrand stretched clear of the three Brits in the second lap of the run and held firm.

It concludes a dominant season for Beaugrand, who has won all five of the World Championship circuit races she entered.

Taylor-Brown won the Czech Republic leg of the series earlier this month, which was her first win on the tour since 2023.

title: England's Harrison scores last-gasp try to beat Black Ferns
description: Zoe Harrison scores last-gasp try as England defeat New Zealand at Allianz Stadium to avoid a second successive draw in the WXV Global Series.
fullText:
Tries: Moloney-MacDonald, Kildunne, Breach, Harrison Cons: Harrison 3

Tries: Du Plessis, Leti-I'iga, Paul Cons: Sorensen-McGee 2

Zoe Harrison scored a last-gasp try as England defeated New Zealand at Allianz Stadium to avoid a second successive draw in the WXV Global Series.

With the scores level at 19-19 in the 81st minute and having missed a penalty moments earlier, Harrison intercepted a pass as the Black Ferns tried to counter-attack, the fly-half diving over the line and piled up on by celebrating team-mates.

The world champions' record 39-game winning run came to an end last weekend in the 26-26 draw with Canada, but this week they were able to find a dramatic path to victory, much to the delight of the 59,871 crowd.

New Zealand, the last team to beat England in the World Cup final in 2022, suffered their first defeat under new head coach Whitney Hansen.

The Black Ferns had taken a deserved lead at half-time after tries from Amy du Plessis and Ayesha Leti-I'iga ruled out Claudia Moloney-MacDonald's opening score.

Tries by Ellie Kildunne and Jess Breach - either side of Marlie Packer having to go off for concussion after being hit hard by a high tackle - restored England's lead.

Mererangi Paul's converted try drew the game level on 70 minutes to set up a grandstand finish.

Red Roses embrace growing competitiveness of game

Rugby Union Weekly: Harrison's last-gasp try seals dramatic England win

The Black Ferns have beaten the Red Roses in all five World Cup final meetings they have contested.

Canada outclassed New Zealand in last year's World Cup semi-final to deny a repeat of what is one of rugby's great rivalries.

Under Hansen, who took over as head coach after last year's disappointing World Cup, the Black Ferns were unbeaten and have defeated Canada and France this year.

The world's second-ranked side spent a large chunk of the first half deep in England's 22, and an opportunistic kick found unmarked space for Du Plessis to dot down for a deserved try.

England comfortably beat New Zealand 49-31 in their most recent meeting in 2024, winning all three encounters since their 2022 World Cup final defeat, which has opened the door for Canada to become the Red Roses' toughest contest.

However, the years were rolled back in Twickenham as Hansen's side brought a fearsome level of physicality and speed to challenge the Red Roses.

Leti-I'iga, who had an opening try ruled out, caused havoc throughout the first half and finally crossed after Tyla King broke clear, before a poorly judged cross-field kick, with another try beckoning, let John Mitchell's side off the hook.

England have not led at half-time in any of their Global WXV Series games.

Given their season only began two weeks ago against Australia, Mitchell has been quick to defend his side's rustiness.

Individual magic from Kildunne, who spotted a gap on the wing for her try, and a yellow card for a high shot by Veisinia Mahutariki-Fakalelu, presented Mitchell with an opportunity to empty his bench with momentum behind his side.

Breach's simple finish came in the next play as any fears of a first loss in four years began to dissolve.

But the Black Ferns refused to go away and continued to trouble England's defence, which is now being influenced by coaching consultant Shaun Edwards.

Mitchell's side were criticised for turning down a kickable penalty late in the game against Canada.

The opportunity again presented itself, and Harrison took it on from distance, but the ball came up well short.

Canada opted to kick the ball out and accept the draw last week, which is not in the DNA of New Zealand, and they attacked from distance in an attempt to inflict England's first loss on home soil since 2016.

That proved to be the wrong decision, as a pass was picked off deep inside the visitors' 22, and instead the Red Roses won their 14th straight game at Allianz Stadium.

title: Australia down Scotland with second-half burst
description: Scotland suffer a third successive defeat in the WXV Global Series as clinical Australia prove too strong in Edinburgh.
fullText:

Scotland suffered a third successive defeat in the WXV Global Series as clinical Australia proved too strong in Edinburgh.

After losses against Canada and New Zealand - ranked two and three in the world - hopes were high the Scots could get off the mark against the side one place below them in the world rankings.

Despite leading 10-5 at the break, Scotland could not live with the rampant Wallaroos, who ran in three tries in a devastating eight-minute second-half spell to secure a comfortable win.

The sides meet again in Sydney next weekend.

Evie Gallagher, following her two tries against New Zealand last weekend, gave Scotland the lead on 15 minutes, dotting down to round off a period of pressure on the Australian line.

The hosts were on top, with Meryl Smith in midfield and lock Holland Bogan carrying hard and asking questions of the Australian defence, but loose work at the line-out cost Dave Butcher's team some promising attacking positions.

The Wallaroos grew into the game as the half wore on and hit back with a well-worked try. Scotland repelled a rolling line-out maul close to their own line, but the visitors remained patient and spun the ball wide for Georgina Friedrichs to put Desiree Miller over in the corner.

The Scots hit back immediately when Australia were penalised for holding on straight from the restart, and Helen Nelson banged over a penalty to give her side a five-point lead at the break.

However, Australia flew out of the blocks after the interval and turned the game on its head with three tries in quick succession.

The first came when a rolling line-out maul was halted just short and scrum-half Samantha Wood was on hand to dive over. She converted her own try to nudge the visitors in front for the first time, and it was a double blow for Scotland as Gallagher was sin-binned for illegally bringing down the initial maul.

With the numerical advantage, the Wallaroos came on strong as Brianna Hoy and then Faitala Moleko cut through to score and put the visitors in charge at 24-10.

Wood knocked over a penalty to put Australia beyond two scores and added another late on to cap off a dominant second half from the Wallaroos.

title: Broken promises, confiscated land: the hyperscale AI datacentre being built in a tiny Indian village
description:

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.

fullText:
Locals say Google’s $15bn project in Andhra Pradesh has resulted in smallholdings being taken back off them by the government

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.

Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.

The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.

Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.

Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.

“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”

Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”

The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.

Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.

But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.

Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.

The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.

But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.

Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.

Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.

Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.

“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.

Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.

“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.

In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.

The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.

Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.

“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”

Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”

For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.

The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.

“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.

Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.

But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.

“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.

“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”

The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.

One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.

“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

title: Norris says Colapinto should be banned after accident
description: World champion Lando Norris calls for Alpine's Franco Colapinto to be banned for causing an accident at a restart at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
fullText:
World champion Lando Norris has called for Alpine's Franco Colapinto to be banned for causing an accident at a restart at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

McLaren's Norris was taken out in a chain reaction when the Argentine locked up his brakes and slid into team-mate Pierre Gasly, who then hit Norris. All three cars retired as a result of the incident.

Norris told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Give him a ban. It's quite simple."

Colapinto said: "I can be sorry to everyone. It's been a big mistake, of course. I just locked up and then I was very out of control."

Briton Norris said he believed governing body the FIA should take such incidents more seriously because of the impact it has on other drivers who are blameless, and the cost in terms of damaged parts.

"The FIA should be more strict and start handing out bans for this kind of stuff," Norris said.

"It's careless from people. It costs a lot of money. All my parts are in the bin now, so people should just get banned for this kind of driving. (They) don't deserve to be in Formula 1.

"If you cause a crash on a restart like this, yeah, you should have at least a one-race ban."

Russell wins despite late Verstappen challenge

However, race winner George Russell and Max Verstappen, who took second, both said a ban would be too severe.

Mercedes' Russell said: "That's too harsh. Safety car restarts, cold tyres, a very small mistake can have big consequences. And from what I saw today, that's what it looked like. It was a small error that had a big consequence. Race bans should come from drivers intentionally doing something very dangerous and very reckless."

Red Bull's Verstappen added: "As long as the driver that caused it is aware of what he did, right, and apologised... It's not nice. Not nice for anyone involved, right? But like George said, a race ban probably is a bit much."

Colapinto was given a 10-second penalty in the race, but as he was already retired this will be converted into a grid drop at the next race, the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, next weekend.

The size of the grid penalty has not been confirmed, but it is likely to be in the order of five places.

Both Alpine drivers were in with a chance of scoring points in the race, and were running seventh and 10th before the incident.

Most galling for the team was that Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad finished seventh and that has extended their gap over Alpine in their fight for fifth place in the constructors' championship to 15 points.

Gasly said he was "crushed" by the incident.

"We're all very disappointed with the outcome after such a strong weekend, strong race," the Frenchman said. "It's still difficult to process what just happened."

A McLaren spokesperson said it was too early to say whether the incident would mean Norris would not be able to use the upgraded parts the team debuted in Baku at the race in Malaysia.

title: Do England have a problem against top-10 teams?
description: As England prepare to take on Spain in their opening Nations League match, BBC Sport takes a look at whether they have a problem when faced with teams in the world top 10.
fullText:
When England take on Spain in their opening Nations League match on Saturday, it will be tinged with a feeling of 'what could have been' for Three Lions fans.

The Wembley match comes three months after England agonisingly missed out on the chance to face La Roja in the World Cup final, having lost to Argentina in the last four.

That would have been a repeat of the 2024 Euros final, which England also lost.

In fact, their record against top-10 sides leaves much to be desired.

In their past 15 matches against sides ranked in the top 10 in the world - according to Fifa's rankings - England have won six matches.

Three of those wins were at major tournaments - the Euros semi-finals in 2021 and 2024 against Denmark and the Netherlands, and the bronze-medal match against France at this summer's World Cup.

The victory over Les Bleus to take third place was Thomas Tuchel's first win as England boss over a top-10 opponent.

And his first win over opposition ranked inside the top 20 came in their opening group game at the tournament against Croatia.

So do England have a problem against top-10 opposition?

Six wins in their past 15 games against top-10 opponents are not the kind of numbers an England team with the ambition of winning major tournaments can be happy with.

Two of those wins meant the Three Lions advanced to the Euro finals of 2020 and 2024. One was in the World Cup match no one wants to play in, two were Euro qualifying matches against an Italy side already on a sharp decline and one came against Belgium in a Nations League match six years ago.

To put it simply, when faced with really elite opposition, England continue to stumble. Particularly at the World Cup.

England have been eliminated every time they have faced a top-10 ranked nation in the knockout stages of the World Cup since 1998 - seven times out of seven.

In their past 10 World Cup games against sides ranked in the top 10, their sole win came in the 2002 group stage against Argentina.

When faced with the defending world champions at the World Cup, they have lost on all four occasions.

England have fared better at the Euros, overcoming top-10 opponents in Denmark and the Netherlands to reach the final at the past two tournaments but ultimately falling at the final hurdle on both occasions against Spain (2024) and Italy (2020).

Meanwhile, their lowest possession in their last 15 games against top-10 opponents came in the semi-final against Argentina (35.8%) at this summer's World Cup and in those Euros finals against Spain (34.9%) and Italy (42.1%).

England's all-time top scorer Kane, with 85 goals, was asked which missing ingredient was needed to get them over the line.

"I think it's just in those biggest moments, still being ourselves," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"The Argentina game was so hard to take, because we had a mindset of going to win the tournament, win in our way and our style, and if we lose trying to do that then we will take that.

"The Argentina game was maybe the first game we tried 'not to lose' in the last 30 minutes and then we ended up losing anyway."

Kane has scored 152 goals in 154 games for Bayern, winning two Bundesliga titles.

"I have experienced it at Bayern Munich for example, you don't fear anyone," the 33-year-old said.

"You go and be yourself, if a team beats you, shake their hand after and say well done.

"You have an identity that you keep throughout.

"I think with England now that is where we need to look.

"We are very close, we have been very close but ultimately, we don't need to fear anyone.

"We just need to be ourselves in the biggest moments and hopefully get over the line."

England have been getting closer to major tournament glory over a number of years but the same question remains - can they dominate the ball and beat elite opposition?

At Euro 2020, the last-16 win over Germany was huge - beating one of the historic footballing powers. But that was a German side in transition who were, at the time, ranked outside the world's top 10.

England were then beaten by Italy in the final after taking the lead, dropping deep and giving up possession before losing on penalties.

At the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, the Three Lions started the tournament with a free-flowing 6-2 win over Iran. Although this was not top opposition, the change in mentality from previous tournaments was notable.

But yet again the same issues resurfaced. Despite largely being the better team against France, a Harry Kane missed penalty and Les Bleus' know-how put England out at the quarter-final stage.

Euro 2024 proved to be one tournament too far for Gareth Southgate and that team did not play anywhere near their best, relying on individual quality to get them through.

A last-gasp Ollie Watkins strike was needed to beat the Netherlands in the semis while Kane was not at full fitness and without him at his best, the team never troubled a formidable Spain side.

After a flawless 2026 World Cup qualifying campaign and a new elite coach in Tuchel, many thought this was England's time for glory.

But, despite showing a huge amount of togetherness and grit in the last-16 win over Mexico, the same old problems once again sunk England.

The Three Lions cannot seem to translate world class talent into ball possession and control of the game, with Tuchel saying he may have to embrace the chaos, and Anthony Gordon adding that England should lean on their traditional direct style.

Perhaps that is what is needed to finally end their long wait for a trophy.

fullText:
A New Mexico jury on Friday found Facebook liable for deceiving users about privacy protections on the platform in the latest legal setback against the social media giant that has already cost it billions of dollars.

The jury found over 43 million violations of state consumer protection law and it is now up to the judge to determine how much the company would pay, with attorneys representing the state asking for the maximum $5,000 penalty per violation.

"The verdict marks a significant victory for New Mexico consumers and holds one of the world's largest technology companies accountable for its conduct," the New Mexico Department of Justice said in a statement.

The two-week trial in Santa Fe centered on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm's clients included the 2016 campaign for Donald Trump.

Jurors sided with prosecutors, finding Facebook made deceptive statements about protecting users' data that affected New Mexico's entire population of more than two million people. The jury also found Facebook misled the public about investigations into third-party app developers that harvest user data following the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

"We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record," said Alex Burgos, a spokesperson for Meta in an email.

During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook claimed the state's evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico found only one other instance of a data breach.

The trial also addressed Facebook's policies for removing harmful content. The state claimed the company favored certain accounts and allowed for violent, or inaccurate, content to proliferate. Facebook denied the claims, arguing the company has adapted its policies since the state's lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it removes 99% of content that violates standards.

The jury reviewed 34 statements made by the company about data protections and content policies, finding the company deceived users about its practices in almost every case.

In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn't prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.

In a deposition played for jurors, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company had robust systems to determine whether content should be taken down. During closing arguments, Randi McGinn, an attorney representing the state, argued that Facebook profited off harmful content, which lawyers for the company denied.

"Meta's platforms are forums for free expression. We have a First Amendment right to manage those platforms in a way we believe best serves the interests of our community. This means prioritizing free speech, protecting our users' information and giving them control over their data," said Burgos.

The judge will decide on penalties at a later date, but that hearing hasn't been set yet. It will be up to the state to decide where the money will go. The state is also seeking an injunction to stop similar practices in the future.

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle a multistate lawsuit involving child safety issues. Buried in the 130-page settlement was an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach, making New Mexico the only state to decide to pursue a case on its own. Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, saying it was not tough enough on Meta, leaving the door open for future litigation.

Also this year, New Mexico won judgments totaling $942 million from Meta in a two-phase trial about the company's safety protections for minors. The court ordered Meta to implement new safeguards, including age-verification technology and time limits on its platforms.

Schuettler reported from Phoenix.

— Schuettler is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.
